Then we add up those 1s as we go, which gives the page number, and finally we total each page.
questions.remember: Mark the breaks with 1, running total gives the session.
questions.why: LAG compares each event with the previous one for the same customer, and the CASE emits 1 at every session boundary, including the first row where LAG is NULL. A running SUM of those flags (default RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING frame) assigns a stable session number that GROUP BY can use. Adding INTERVAL '30' MINUTE to a DATE avoids floating-point issues from comparing date differences with 30/1440.
questions.tip: For sessionization I flag boundaries with LAG and turn them into group ids with a running SUM, the same trick used for gaps and islands.

questions.title: Asset class roll-rate matrix
questions.scenario: Rohit Agarwal in credit risk prepares a monthly roll-rate matrix for the risk committee, showing how loans moved between Standard, SMA-1, SMA-2 and NPA buckets. Loans closed during October have no October row and must show up as CLOSED, not vanish.
questions.schema:
CLASS_SEP(loan_id VARCHAR2(10), asset_class VARCHAR2(6), outstanding NUMBER(14,2))
-- classification as on 30-09-2026
CLASS_OCT(loan_id VARCHAR2(10), asset_class VARCHAR2(6), outstanding NUMBER(14,2))
-- classification as on 31-10-2026; asset_class STD, SMA1, SMA2 or NPA; outstanding in INR
questions.task: Build a matrix with one row per September class and one count column per October class (STD, SMA1, SMA2, NPA, CLOSED), rows ordered STD, SMA1, SMA2.
questions.hint: LEFT JOIN September to October, use NVL to label missing October rows as 'CLOSED', then PIVOT COUNT(*) on the October class.
questions.solution:
SELECT *
FROM  (SELECT s.asset_class AS sep_class,
              NVL(o.asset_class, 'CLOSED') AS oct_class
       FROM   class_sep s
       LEFT   JOIN class_oct o ON o.loan_id = s.loan_id)
PIVOT (COUNT(*) FOR oct_class IN ('STD' AS std, 'SMA1' AS sma1,
                                  'SMA2' AS sma2, 'NPA' AS npa,
                                  'CLOSED' AS closed))
ORDER BY DECODE(sep_class, 'STD', 1, 'SMA1', 2, 'SMA2', 3, 'NPA', 4);
questions.simple: Think of a class photo taken in September and again in October, where children may have changed sections. We make a table: rows are the September section, columns are the October section, and each box counts how many children moved that way. A child who left the school is put in a 'left' column instead of being forgotten. PIVOT turns the October section values into those columns.
questions.remember: Rows = where you were, columns = where you went.
questions.why: The LEFT JOIN keeps every September loan, and NVL maps the missing October side to 'CLOSED' so attrition is counted. PIVOT groups implicitly by every column of the source not mentioned in the PIVOT clause (here only sep_class) and returns 0 for COUNT where no rows exist. DECODE in ORDER BY imposes the business order of buckets instead of alphabetical order.
questions.tip: In a PIVOT I select only the columns I want as row keys in the inline view, because every other column becomes an implicit GROUP BY key.

questions.title: Migrate MF transactions, log bad rows
questions.scenario: Swati Kapoor is migrating legacy mutual fund transactions into the new RTA platform. Some legacy rows break constraints, and she wants the good rows loaded in one INSERT while every bad row is captured with its Oracle error for the business to fix.
questions.schema:
LEGACY_MF_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), folio_no VARCHAR2(10), scheme_code VARCHAR2(10), txn_type VARCHAR2(1), amount NUMBER(14,2))
-- staging copy of the old system, no constraints
MF_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10) PRIMARY KEY, folio_no VARCHAR2(10) NOT NULL, scheme_code VARCHAR2(10), txn_type VARCHAR2(1) CHECK (txn_type IN ('P','R')), amount NUMBER(14,2) CHECK (amount > 0))
-- P = purchase, R = redemption, amount in INR
questions.output_note: ERR$_MF_TXN after the load. MF_TXN now holds 2 rows (M9001 and M9004). 1 = unique key (duplicate M9001), 1400 = NULL folio_no, 2290 = check constraint on amount or txn_type.
questions.task: Create an error log table for MF_TXN with DBMS_ERRLOG, load all rows from LEGACY_MF_TXN in a single INSERT that logs failing rows with the tag 'MIG_1611' instead of stopping, commit, and list the logged errors.
questions.hint: DBMS_ERRLOG.CREATE_ERROR_LOG creates ERR$_MF_TXN; add LOG ERRORS INTO err$_mf_txn ('MIG_1611') REJECT LIMIT UNLIMITED to the INSERT.
questions.simple: Think of a teacher checking homework copies one by one. Without error logging, one bad copy makes her throw away the whole pile. With LOG ERRORS she keeps the good copies and puts each bad one in a separate tray with a note saying what was wrong. Here the good fund transactions go into MF_TXN, and the bad ones go into ERR$_MF_TXN with their Oracle error number.
questions.remember: LOG ERRORS = good rows in, bad rows aside.
questions.why: DML error logging lets a single set-based INSERT, UPDATE, MERGE or DELETE skip rows that raise errors such as NOT NULL, CHECK, unique or conversion failures and record them, with ORA_ERR_NUMBER$, ORA_ERR_MESG$ and the tag, in the ERR$_ table. Without it, one bad row rolls back the whole statement, forcing slow row-by-row loops. The error table columns are VARCHAR2(4000), so even values that failed conversion can be stored, and the log rows persist even if the main transaction is rolled back.
questions.tip: For migrations I use LOG ERRORS REJECT LIMIT UNLIMITED so the load stays set-based and the business gets a clean list of rejected rows with reasons.

questions.title: Flatten broker trade confirmations
questions.scenario: Deepak Shetty in the back office of a stock broking firm receives exchange trade confirmations from an API as JSON. One order can be filled in several parts, and he needs one row per fill for the contract note, while rejected orders with no fills must still be visible.
questions.schema:
BROKER_CONFIRM(msg_id VARCHAR2(10), payload CLOB CHECK (payload IS JSON))
-- payload keys: trade_id, symbol, side (B/S), optional fills array of {qty, price}; price in INR
questions.output_note: BC3 has no fills array, but NESTED PATH behaves like an outer join, so the parent row still appears with NULL fill columns.
questions.task: Return one row per fill with msg_id, trade_id, symbol, side, fill_no (position in the array), qty, price and fill_value = qty * price, ordered by msg_id and fill_no.
questions.hint: Use JSON_TABLE with '$' for the order-level columns and NESTED PATH '$.fills[*]' with FOR ORDINALITY for the fills.
questions.solution:
SELECT b.msg_id, j.trade_id, j.symbol, j.side,
       j.fill_no, j.qty, j.price, j.qty * j.price AS fill_value
FROM   broker_confirm b,
       JSON_TABLE(b.payload, '$'
         COLUMNS (
           trade_id VARCHAR2(10) PATH '$.trade_id',
           symbol   VARCHAR2(20) PATH '$.symbol',
           side     VARCHAR2(1)  PATH '$.side',
           NESTED PATH '$.fills[*]'
             COLUMNS (
               fill_no FOR ORDINALITY,
               qty     NUMBER PATH '$.qty',
               price   NUMBER PATH '$.price'
             )
         )) j
ORDER  BY b.msg_id, j.fill_no;
questions.simple: Think of a tiffin box with an outer lid and small boxes inside. JSON_TABLE opens the lid and reads the label on top (trade, share, buy or sell). NESTED PATH then opens each small box inside, one row per small box, and FOR ORDINALITY numbers them 1, 2, 3. If a tiffin has no small boxes, we still write down its label with empty values, so nothing goes missing.
questions.remember: JSON_TABLE opens the box; NESTED PATH opens boxes inside.
questions.why: JSON_TABLE projects JSON into relational columns and is implicitly lateral, so it can reference b.payload from the same FROM clause. A NESTED PATH produces one child row per array element and is joined to its parent with outer-join semantics, so documents without the array still return one row with NULL child columns. FOR ORDINALITY gives the element's position, which is handy for ordering fills.
questions.tip: For arrays inside JSON I use NESTED PATH in JSON_TABLE rather than calling JSON_TABLE twice, because it keeps parents without children.

questions.title: Daily lowest and highest call rate
questions.scenario: Arvind Kulkarni on the treasury desk borrows and lends overnight in the call money market. Before the morning ALCO call he wants to see, for each day, the cheapest and the costliest rate at which deals were done.
questions.schema:
CALL_MONEY_DEAL(deal_id VARCHAR2(10), deal_date DATE, counterparty VARCHAR2(40), amount_cr NUMBER(10,2), rate_pct NUMBER(5,2))
-- amount_cr = deal amount in INR crore, rate_pct = annual interest rate in %
questions.task: For each deal date show the lowest and the highest rate_pct, sorted by date.
questions.hint: Group by deal_date and use MIN(rate_pct) and MAX(rate_pct) in the SELECT list.
questions.solution:
SELECT deal_date,
       MIN(rate_pct) AS min_rate,
       MAX(rate_pct) AS max_rate
FROM   call_money_deal
GROUP  BY deal_date
ORDER  BY deal_date;
questions.simple: Think of a class where every child writes their height on the board each day. MIN finds the shortest child and MAX finds the tallest child. GROUP BY deal_date makes a separate little group for each day. So for every day we get the lowest rate and the highest rate in one line.
questions.remember: MIN = smallest, MAX = biggest, GROUP BY = one row per group.
questions.why: MIN and MAX are aggregate functions, so GROUP BY deal_date collapses all deals of a day into one row and computes both in a single scan. Like other aggregates they ignore NULL values, and they also work on dates and strings. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must appear in GROUP BY.
questions.tip: MIN and MAX work on numbers, dates and text, and they skip NULLs just like SUM and AVG.

questions.title: Health claims still waiting for settlement
questions.scenario: Pooja Menon heads claims operations at a health insurer. IRDAI wants claims settled quickly, so every morning she needs the list of claims that have no settlement date yet.
questions.schema:
HEALTH_CLAIM(claim_id VARCHAR2(10), policy_no VARCHAR2(12), claim_amt NUMBER(12,2), intimated_on DATE, settled_on DATE)
-- claim_amt in INR, settled_on is NULL until the claim is paid
questions.task: List the claims that are not settled yet, oldest intimation first.
questions.hint: settled_on = NULL is never true; write settled_on IS NULL instead.
questions.solution:
SELECT claim_id, policy_no, claim_amt, intimated_on
FROM   health_claim
WHERE  settled_on IS NULL
ORDER  BY intimated_on;
questions.simple: Think of a school register where the 'returned book on' box is empty for some children. An empty box is not equal to anything, not even to another empty box. So asking 'is the box = empty?' never says yes. In SQL we must ask 'IS NULL', which means 'is this box empty?'. That gives us the claims with no settlement date.
questions.remember: Empty box? Ask IS NULL, never = NULL.
questions.why: NULL means unknown, so any comparison with NULL using =, <> or > evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows that are TRUE. That is why WHERE settled_on = NULL returns no rows without raising an error. IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the only predicates that test for missing values directly.
questions.tip: I never write = NULL; comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN, so I use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

questions.title: Senior citizen FD rate eligibility
questions.scenario: Nikhil Bhosale runs the fixed deposit product at a private bank. Customers aged 60 or more get an extra 0.50% on FDs, and he wants each customer's exact age on 17-11-2026 so the rate is right even for someone whose birthday is that very day.
questions.schema:
FD_CUSTOMER(cust_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_name VARCHAR2(60), dob DATE)
-- dob = date of birth
questions.task: Show each customer's age in completed years on 17-11-2026 and label them 'Senior' if the age is 60 or more, else 'Regular'.
questions.hint: TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2026-11-17', dob) / 12) gives completed years; dividing days by 365 goes wrong around birthdays.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, cust_name,
       TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2026-11-17', dob) / 12) AS age,
       CASE WHEN MONTHS_BETWEEN(DATE '2026-11-17', dob) >= 720
            THEN 'Senior' ELSE 'Regular' END AS category
FROM   fd_customer
ORDER  BY cust_id;
questions.simple: Think of counting birthdays on a calendar instead of counting days. If your birthday is today, you have just finished one more year. MONTHS_BETWEEN counts how many months have passed since you were born, and dividing by 12 gives years. TRUNC cuts off the half-finished year, so 59 and a bit stays 59. Ramesh turns 60 today and is Senior, but Sunita turns 60 tomorrow and is still Regular.
questions.remember: Age = TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(today, dob) / 12).
questions.why: MONTHS_BETWEEN returns a whole number when both dates fall on the same day of the month, so a birthday on the reference date gives exactly 720 months and age 60. Calculations like (date - dob)/365 drift because of leap years and can label someone 60 a day or two early or late. TRUNC rather than ROUND is needed because age counts only completed years.
questions.tip: For age I use TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(ref_date, dob)/12) because dividing days by 365 breaks around birthdays and leap years.

questions.title: Turn branch return columns into rows
questions.scenario: Farhan Qureshi prepares the monthly branch return that feeds an RBI submission. The return table has one column per figure, but the validation tool needs one row per branch per figure, and a missing figure must still appear so the reviewer can chase the branch.
questions.schema:
BRANCH_RETURN(branch_code VARCHAR2(6), deposits_cr NUMBER(12,2), advances_cr NUMBER(12,2), npa_cr NUMBER(12,2))
-- October 2026 figures in INR crore; NULL = branch has not submitted that figure
questions.task: Return branch_code, metric ('DEPOSITS', 'ADVANCES' or 'NPA') and value_cr, one row per branch per metric, keeping rows where the value is missing. Sort by branch_code and metric.
questions.hint: UNPIVOT drops NULL values by default; add INCLUDE NULLS to keep B102's missing NPA row.
questions.solution:
SELECT branch_code, metric, value_cr
FROM   branch_return
UNPIVOT INCLUDE NULLS (
  value_cr FOR metric IN (deposits_cr AS 'DEPOSITS',
                          advances_cr AS 'ADVANCES',
                          npa_cr      AS 'NPA')
)
ORDER  BY branch_code, metric;
questions.simple: Think of a marks card where each subject is written side by side in one line. UNPIVOT rewrites it as a list, one line per subject, like 'Maths 80', 'Science 75'. Normally, if a subject has no mark, that line is quietly left out. INCLUDE NULLS keeps the empty line, so the teacher can see that a mark is missing.
questions.remember: UNPIVOT = columns to rows; INCLUDE NULLS keeps the blanks.
questions.why: UNPIVOT rotates the listed columns into two columns: one holding the value and one holding a label for the source column. By default it uses EXCLUDE NULLS, which silently removes rows whose value is NULL, so a missing regulatory figure would vanish instead of being flagged. Before UNPIVOT existed this was done with UNION ALL of one SELECT per column, which scans the table once per column.
questions.tip: UNPIVOT excludes NULLs by default, so for validation reports I add INCLUDE NULLS so missing figures stay visible.

questions.title: Flag card spends far above recent average
questions.scenario: Meera Pillai in the card fraud team wants a simple velocity rule: a swipe is suspicious if it is more than 3 times the average of that card's previous 3 swipes. The current swipe must not be part of its own average, and a card's first swipe has no history.
questions.schema:
CARD_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), card_no VARCHAR2(16), txn_time DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- card_no is masked, amount in INR, txn_time includes the time
questions.task: For every transaction show the average of the same card's previous 3 transactions (rounded to 2 decimals) and a flag 'Y' when amount is more than 3 times that average, else 'N'.
questions.hint: Use AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card_no ORDER BY txn_time ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) so the frame stops just before the current row.
questions.solution:
SELECT txn_id, card_no, amount,
       ROUND(prev3_avg, 2) AS prev3_avg,
       CASE WHEN amount > 3 * prev3_avg THEN 'Y' ELSE 'N' END AS suspicious
FROM  (SELECT t.*,
              AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card_no ORDER BY txn_time
                                ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS prev3_avg
       FROM   card_txn t)
ORDER  BY card_no, txn_time;
questions.simple: Think of checking your shopping bills in a passbook. For each new bill, you cover it with your hand and look only at the 3 bills just above it. You work out their average and ask, 'is this new bill more than 3 times that?'. The very first bill has nothing above it, so there is no average and it is not flagged.
questions.remember: 1 PRECEDING ends the frame just before me.
questions.why: The frame ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING excludes the current row, so a large swipe cannot dilute its own baseline. Near the start of a partition the frame holds fewer than 3 rows (T807 averages only T806) and for the first row it is empty, so AVG returns NULL and the comparison is UNKNOWN, which falls to the ELSE branch. ROWS is used rather than RANGE so the frame counts physical rows, not time distance.
questions.tip: To compare a value with its own history I end the frame at 1 PRECEDING, otherwise the current row pollutes the baseline.

questions.title: Roll balances up the GL tree
questions.scenario: Sandeep Agarwal in finance control reconciles the trial balance with the balance sheet heads. The chart of accounts is a tree, balances sit mostly on leaf GLs (and sometimes on a parent by mistake), and he needs every GL's total including all accounts below it.
questions.schema:
GL_ACCOUNT(gl_code VARCHAR2(6), gl_name VARCHAR2(40), parent_gl VARCHAR2(6))
-- parent_gl is NULL for the top account
GL_BALANCE(gl_code VARCHAR2(6), balance NUMBER(16,2))
-- closing balance in INR posted directly to that GL
questions.task: For every GL account show its total balance: its own posted balance plus the balances of all accounts below it at any depth. Sort by gl_code.
questions.hint: Run CONNECT BY without START WITH so every account becomes a root, keep CONNECT_BY_ROOT gl_code, then LEFT JOIN balances and group by the root.
questions.solution:
SELECT a.gl_code, a.gl_name,
       SUM(NVL(b.balance, 0)) AS total_balance
FROM  (SELECT CONNECT_BY_ROOT gl_code AS root_gl, gl_code
       FROM   gl_account
       CONNECT BY PRIOR gl_code = parent_gl) t
JOIN   gl_account a ON a.gl_code = t.root_gl
LEFT JOIN gl_balance b ON b.gl_code = t.gl_code
GROUP  BY a.gl_code, a.gl_name
ORDER  BY a.gl_code;
questions.simple: Think of cupboard drawers inside bigger drawers. To know how much money is in a big drawer, you add its own coins plus the coins in every small drawer inside it. The query starts a walk from every drawer, writes down where the walk started, and collects every drawer it reaches. Then it adds up the coins for each starting drawer.
questions.remember: CONNECT_BY_ROOT = remember where the walk started.
questions.why: Omitting START WITH makes every row a root, so the hierarchy is expanded once per account and each descendant row carries CONNECT_BY_ROOT, the root it was reached from. Grouping by that root sums a whole subtree, including balances posted directly on non-leaf GLs like 1200. The LEFT JOIN with NVL keeps accounts whose own row has no balance.
questions.tip: For subtree totals I use CONNECT BY without START WITH and group by CONNECT_BY_ROOT, which gives every node its full rolled-up balance in one query.

questions.title: Live client positions with a materialized view
questions.scenario: Rahul Saxena runs risk at a stock broker. The margin screen recalculates net positions from the full TRADE table every few seconds and is slowing down, so he wants a materialized view that keeps net quantity per client and stock and updates itself on every commit.
questions.schema:
TRADE(trade_id VARCHAR2(10), trade_date DATE, client_id VARCHAR2(8), symbol VARCHAR2(12), side VARCHAR2(1), qty NUMBER(10), price NUMBER(12,2))
-- side B = buy, S = sell; price in INR per share
questions.output_note: CLIENT_POSITION_MV right after it is built. CL02 HDFCBANK stays with net 0 because the group still has trades. When a new trade commits, only the changed group is updated using the MV log.
questions.task: Create a materialized view log on TRADE and a REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT materialized view CLIENT_POSITION_MV with net quantity (buys minus sells) and trade count per client and symbol, then query it.
questions.hint: For a fast-refreshable aggregate MV, SUM(expr) must be accompanied by COUNT(expr) and COUNT(*), and the log needs ROWID, SEQUENCE, the used columns and INCLUDING NEW VALUES.
questions.solution:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW LOG ON trade
  WITH ROWID, SEQUENCE (client_id, symbol, side, qty)
  INCLUDING NEW VALUES;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW client_position_mv
  BUILD IMMEDIATE
  REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT
AS
SELECT client_id, symbol,
       SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'B' THEN qty ELSE -qty END)   AS net_qty,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN side = 'B' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS net_qty_cnt,
       COUNT(*)                                           AS trade_cnt
FROM   trade
GROUP  BY client_id, symbol;

SELECT client_id, symbol, net_qty, trade_cnt
FROM   client_position_mv
ORDER  BY client_id, symbol;
questions.simple: Think of a piggy bank with a small notebook beside it. Instead of counting every coin again each time, you write down each coin you add or take out, and then just fix the total. The MV log is that notebook, and the materialized view is the saved total. REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT means the total is fixed the moment a trade is saved.
questions.remember: MV log notes the changes; fast refresh fixes only those.
questions.why: A materialized view stores the query result as a table, so the margin screen reads a few summary rows instead of aggregating all trades. The MV log records changed rows, and with COUNT(*) and COUNT(expr) present Oracle can apply inserts, updates and deletes incrementally, even removing a group when its count reaches zero. ON COMMIT adds a little work to each trade commit, so for very high trade volumes ON DEMAND refresh at short intervals may be chosen instead; DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW shows whether fast refresh is possible.
questions.tip: Before promising fast refresh I check DBMS_MVIEW.EXPLAIN_MVIEW, and I always add COUNT(*) and COUNT(expr) next to SUM so Oracle can refresh incrementally.

questions.concept: SKIP LOCKED with BULK COLLECT LIMIT
questions.title: Parallel workers picking NEFT payments
questions.scenario: Ankita Deshmukh supports the outward NEFT engine, where several worker sessions pick pending payments from one table. Worker W1 has already locked N901 and N902 and not committed yet; worker W2 must take the next 3 free payments without waiting and without touching W1's rows.
questions.schema:
NEFT_OUTWARD(pay_id VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(14,2), status VARCHAR2(10), worker_id VARCHAR2(5))
-- status PENDING, SENT or FAILED; amount in INR; worker_id = session that sent it
questions.output_note: NEFT_OUTWARD after W2's block commits (W1 still holds N901 and N902). With WHERE ROWNUM <= 3 instead of LIMIT 3, W2 would get only N903, because ROWNUM would pick N901-N903 first and then skip the two locked ones.
questions.task: Write W2's PL/SQL block: lock up to 3 PENDING payments in pay_id order, skipping rows locked by other sessions, mark them SENT with worker_id 'W2', and commit.
questions.hint: Open a FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED cursor and FETCH ... BULK COLLECT LIMIT 3; do not use ROWNUM <= 3, because ROWNUM is applied before locked rows are skipped.
questions.simple: Think of children picking homework copies from a pile to check. If a friend is already holding a copy, you do not stand and wait, you just take the next free one. SKIP LOCKED does exactly that for table rows. LIMIT 3 means 'keep picking until you have 3 free copies', so W2 gets N903, N905 and N906.
questions.remember: SKIP LOCKED = take the next free one, don't wait.
questions.why: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED locks rows as they are fetched and silently passes over rows locked by other sessions, so many workers can drain one queue table without blocking each other. Because ROWNUM (or FETCH FIRST) is evaluated before the lock attempt, a ROWNUM <= 3 filter can return fewer rows than asked when some are locked, so the batch size must be controlled with BULK COLLECT LIMIT on the open cursor. The locks are held until COMMIT, so closing the cursor before the FORALL update is safe.
questions.tip: For queue tables I use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with BULK COLLECT LIMIT, not ROWNUM, because ROWNUM is applied before locked rows are skipped.

questions.title: Monthly UPI count and value
questions.scenario: Rahul Iyer in the digital payments team sends NPCI-style monthly volume numbers to management. He wants the number and total value of successful UPI payments for each month.
questions.schema:
UPI_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), txn_time DATE, payer_vpa VARCHAR2(40), amount NUMBER(12,2), status VARCHAR2(10))
-- txn_time has date and time, amount in INR, status SUCCESS or FAILED
questions.task: For each month show the month as 'YYYY-MM', the count of SUCCESS payments and their total amount, oldest month first.
questions.hint: Use TO_CHAR(txn_time, 'YYYY-MM') both in the SELECT list and in GROUP BY.
questions.solution:
SELECT TO_CHAR(txn_time, 'YYYY-MM') AS txn_month,
       COUNT(*)                     AS txn_count,
       SUM(amount)                  AS total_amt
FROM   upi_txn
WHERE  status = 'SUCCESS'
GROUP  BY TO_CHAR(txn_time, 'YYYY-MM')
ORDER  BY txn_month;
questions.simple: Think of a passbook where every line has a full date like 19 August 2026. If you only look at the month part, all August lines fall into one August pile. TO_CHAR(txn_time, 'YYYY-MM') cuts the date down to just year and month. GROUP BY then makes one pile per month, and COUNT and SUM tell how many and how much.
questions.remember: Cut the date to 'YYYY-MM', then group the piles.
questions.why: TO_CHAR with a 'YYYY-MM' mask turns every DATE in a month into the same string, so GROUP BY on that expression gives one row per month. The same expression must appear in GROUP BY because the column alias is not visible there in Oracle 19c. 'YYYY-MM' strings also sort in calendar order, unlike 'MON-YYYY'.
questions.tip: For monthly reports I group by TRUNC(date,'MM') or TO_CHAR(date,'YYYY-MM'), never by 'MON-YY', because that sorts alphabetically.

questions.title: Customer count per city, cleaned
questions.scenario: Shalini Rao runs the KYC re-verification drive and needs customers per city to plan staff. Branches typed the city in different ways, like ' Mumbai', 'MUMBAI' and 'mumbai ', so a plain GROUP BY shows the same city many times.
questions.schema:
KYC_CUSTOMER(cust_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_name VARCHAR2(60), city VARCHAR2(40))
-- city typed by branch staff, may have extra spaces or mixed case
questions.task: Count customers per city, treating different letter case and extra spaces as the same city. Show the city in capitals, biggest count first.
questions.hint: Group by UPPER(TRIM(city)) so ' Mumbai' and 'mumbai ' become the same 'MUMBAI'.
questions.solution:
SELECT UPPER(TRIM(city)) AS city,
       COUNT(*)          AS customers
FROM   kyc_customer
GROUP  BY UPPER(TRIM(city))
ORDER  BY customers DESC, city;
questions.simple: Think of a school register where one teacher writes ' Mumbai', another writes 'MUMBAI' and a third writes 'mumbai '. To a computer these look like three different words. TRIM cuts off the extra spaces at the start and end. UPPER turns every letter into a capital letter. After that they all say 'MUMBAI', so GROUP BY counts them together.
questions.remember: TRIM the spaces, UPPER the letters, then count.
questions.why: String comparison in Oracle is case-sensitive and counts leading and trailing spaces, so ' Mumbai' and 'MUMBAI' land in different groups. Grouping by the expression UPPER(TRIM(city)) normalises the value before grouping. In migrations the better fix is to clean the column once, or add a check constraint, instead of normalising in every query.
questions.tip: When counts look split, I check for case and space differences with GROUP BY UPPER(TRIM(col)) and then clean the source data.

questions.title: On-time EMIs when payments have times
questions.scenario: Deepak Nair in retail loan collections reports how many EMIs were paid on time for the bureau update. An EMI paid at any time on the due date is on time, but his first query counted the 18:30 payment on 05-09-2026 as late.
questions.schema:
EMI_PAYMENT(loan_id VARCHAR2(10), emi_amt NUMBER(12,2), due_date DATE, paid_on DATE)
-- due_date has no time (midnight), paid_on has date and time of payment, amounts in INR
questions.output_note: A naive paid_on <= due_date would give only 1 on-time EMI per loan, because 05-09-2026 18:30 and 10-08-2026 09:15 are later than midnight of the due date.
questions.task: For each loan count EMIs paid on or before the due date (any time that day counts) and EMIs paid late.
questions.hint: Remove the time part with TRUNC(paid_on) before comparing it with due_date.
questions.solution:
SELECT loan_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN TRUNC(paid_on) <= due_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS on_time_emis,
       SUM(CASE WHEN TRUNC(paid_on) >  due_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS late_emis
FROM   emi_payment
GROUP  BY loan_id
ORDER  BY loan_id;
questions.simple: Think of a stopwatch that starts at midnight. Oracle stores the due date as 'the very first second of 5 September'. A payment at 6:30 in the evening is many hours after that first second, so a plain comparison calls it late. TRUNC rubs out the clock time and keeps only the day. Then 5 September equals 5 September and the EMI is on time.
questions.remember: Dates hide a clock; TRUNC rubs the clock off.
questions.why: An Oracle DATE always carries hours, minutes and seconds, and a date literal or date-only value means 00:00:00. So paid_on <= due_date is false for any payment made later on the due day. TRUNC(paid_on) compares whole days; in a WHERE clause on an indexed column, paid_on < due_date + 1 gives the same result and keeps the index usable.
questions.tip: Every Oracle DATE has a time part, so for 'same day' checks I use TRUNC or a < date + 1 range.

questions.title: Typical SIP amount per scheme
questions.scenario: Farhan Qureshi in the AMC's product team wants the typical monthly SIP per scheme for a distributor presentation. One HNI's ₹50,000 SIP pulls the average far above what most investors pay, and one scheme has an even number of SIPs.
questions.schema:
SIP_MANDATE(scheme_code VARCHAR2(10), investor_id VARCHAR2(10), sip_amount NUMBER(10,2))
-- one active SIP per row, sip_amount = monthly instalment in INR
questions.output_note: AXBLUE has 4 SIPs, so the median is the average of the two middle values (2000 and 5000) = 3500.
questions.task: For each scheme show the average SIP (rounded to whole rupees) and the median SIP.
questions.hint: Oracle has a MEDIAN aggregate; with an even count it averages the two middle values.
questions.solution:
SELECT scheme_code,
       ROUND(AVG(sip_amount)) AS avg_sip,
       MEDIAN(sip_amount)     AS median_sip
FROM   sip_mandate
GROUP  BY scheme_code
ORDER  BY scheme_code;
questions.simple: Think of a class photo where children stand in a line from shortest to tallest. The median is the child standing in the middle. If there are 4 children, there is no single middle, so you take the halfway point between the two in the middle. One very tall child changes the average a lot, but hardly moves the middle. That is why the median shows the 'typical' SIP better.
questions.remember: Median = the middle of the line, not the average.
questions.why: AVG is pulled by outliers, so one ₹50,000 SIP makes AXBLUE look like a ₹14,500 scheme. MEDIAN sorts the values in each group and returns the middle one, or the mean of the two middle values when the count is even; it is the same as PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY sip_amount). Like other aggregates it ignores NULLs and can also be used as an analytic function with OVER (PARTITION BY ...).
questions.tip: When data is skewed, like loan sizes or SIP amounts, I report MEDIAN or PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) along with AVG.

questions.title: Split salary file into capped batches
questions.scenario: Manoj Pillai in corporate cash management sends a client's salary file to NEFT in batches. The client's maker-checker rule says no batch may exceed ₹3,00,000, so rows must be packed in file order and a new batch starts as soon as the next row would cross the cap.
questions.schema:
SALARY_PAYOUT(file_seq NUMBER, emp_id VARCHAR2(10), net_pay NUMBER(12,2))
-- file_seq = row order in the client's file, net_pay in INR, every row is <= 300000
questions.task: Give each row a batch number so that rows stay in file_seq order and each batch total stays at or below 300000. Show the final total of each batch on every row.
questions.hint: A plain running SUM cannot restart; use MATCH_RECOGNIZE with PATTERN (a+) and DEFINE a AS SUM(a.net_pay) <= 300000 (or a recursive WITH).
questions.solution:
SELECT file_seq, emp_id, net_pay, batch_no, batch_total
FROM   salary_payout
MATCH_RECOGNIZE (
  ORDER BY file_seq
  MEASURES MATCH_NUMBER()     AS batch_no,
           FINAL SUM(net_pay) AS batch_total
  ALL ROWS PER MATCH
  PATTERN (a+)
  DEFINE a AS SUM(a.net_pay) <= 300000
)
ORDER  BY file_seq;
questions.simple: Think of filling school bags with books, where each bag can hold only 3 kg. You put books in one by one in order. When the next book would make the bag too heavy, you close that bag and start a new one. MATCH_RECOGNIZE does this: it keeps adding rows while the total stays under the cap, then starts a fresh batch. MATCH_NUMBER tells which bag each row went into.
questions.remember: Bag full? Close it, start a new bag.
questions.why: A windowed SUM cannot reset, because whether a row starts a new batch depends on the running total of the current batch, which depends on earlier decisions. In MATCH_RECOGNIZE the DEFINE condition SUM(a.net_pay) is evaluated as a running sum over the rows already mapped in the current match, so the greedy a+ stops just before the cap is crossed and the next match starts there. FINAL SUM gives the whole batch total on every row with ALL ROWS PER MATCH, while the default RUNNING semantics would show a running total.
questions.tip: Capped running totals that reset need MATCH_RECOGNIZE or a recursive WITH, because analytic SUM cannot restart based on its own result.

questions.title: Daily cash grid with missing reports
questions.scenario: Lakshmi Venkatesh compiles the currency chest balance return for RBI, which needs a row for every branch for every day. Some branches skipped a day, and a normal outer join to a calendar cannot show which branch missed which date.
questions.schema:
BRANCH_CASH(branch_code VARCHAR2(10), bal_date DATE, cash_balance NUMBER(15,2))
-- one row per branch per reported day, bal_date has no time, cash_balance in INR
questions.task: For every branch and every date from 02-11-2026 to 06-11-2026 show the cash balance and a status of REPORTED or MISSING.
questions.hint: Build a 5-day calendar with CONNECT BY LEVEL in a WITH clause, then join it using PARTITION BY (branch_code) RIGHT OUTER JOIN.
questions.solution:
WITH cal AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-02' + LEVEL - 1 AS rpt_date
  FROM   dual
  CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 5
)
SELECT b.branch_code,
       c.rpt_date,
       b.cash_balance,
       CASE WHEN b.bal_date IS NULL THEN 'MISSING' ELSE 'REPORTED' END AS status
FROM   branch_cash b PARTITION BY (b.branch_code)
       RIGHT OUTER JOIN cal c
       ON (b.bal_date = c.rpt_date)
ORDER  BY b.branch_code, c.rpt_date;
questions.simple: Think of a school attendance register with every child's name down the side and every date across the top. Some boxes are empty because the child was absent. A partitioned outer join draws the full grid for each branch, one row per branch per day. Where the branch sent nothing, the box stays empty and we write MISSING.
questions.remember: PARTITION BY join = full register grid for each branch.
questions.why: A plain outer join to the calendar fills gaps only once for the whole table, so a date reported by any branch never appears as missing for another. PARTITION BY (branch_code) on the outer-joined side makes Oracle repeat the outer join for each branch partition, producing the branch × date grid and filling branch_code even on the generated rows. It avoids a manual CROSS JOIN of distinct branches with the calendar.
questions.tip: To densify sparse data per entity I use a partitioned outer join, which is Oracle's built-in way to fill gaps per partition.

questions.title: Stop lost updates on UPI limits
questions.scenario: Gaurav Malhotra maintains the branch screen where staff change a customer's daily UPI limit. Teller T1 and teller T2 both opened C100 at version 3; T1 saved first, and T2 must not silently overwrite T1's change with a stale screen.
questions.schema:
CUST_LIMIT(cust_id VARCHAR2(10), daily_upi_limit NUMBER(12,2), version_no NUMBER, updated_by VARCHAR2(10))
-- daily_upi_limit in INR, version_no increases by 1 on every change
questions.output_note: CUST_LIMIT after the test block. The first call commits C101; the second call raises ORA-20001: Record changed by another user. Please refresh and retry. C100 keeps T1's value.
questions.task: Write procedure update_upi_limit(cust_id, new_limit, read_version, user) that updates only if the version is still the one the screen read, raises ORA-20001 otherwise, and commits on success. Then T2 calls it for C101 (read version 1, new limit 75000) and for C100 (read version 3, new limit 200000).
questions.hint: Put version_no = p_read_version in the UPDATE's WHERE clause and check SQL%ROWCOUNT right after it.
questions.simple: Think of a shared class notebook with a page number written at the top that goes up every time someone edits it. You copy page 3 to your desk to make changes. When you come back, you check: is it still page 3? If a friend already changed it to page 4, you must not scribble over their work, so you stop and read it again. The version number in the WHERE clause is that page check.
questions.remember: Save only if the version is still what I read.
questions.why: Optimistic locking avoids holding row locks while a user looks at a screen: the row is read with its version, and the later UPDATE includes version_no = :read_version, so it updates zero rows if anyone changed it in between. SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0 then signals a conflict and the procedure raises a user-defined error instead of losing T1's update. Pessimistic SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is better for short server-side transactions like transfers, while version columns suit web and teller screens with think time.
questions.tip: For screens with user think time I use optimistic locking with a version column and SQL%ROWCOUNT, and SELECT FOR UPDATE only for short server-side transactions.

questions.title: Route cash deposits to CTR and review
questions.scenario: Sunita Bhattacharya in the AML cell prepares the Cash Transaction Report for FIU-IND. From one day's cash transactions, amounts of ₹10 lakh or more go to the CTR table, and amounts from ₹9 lakh up to just below ₹10 lakh go to a near-threshold table for structuring review, each row to only one table.
questions.schema:
CASH_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_id VARCHAR2(10), txn_type VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(14,2), txn_date DATE)
CTR_REPORT(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_id VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(14,2))
NEAR_THRESHOLD(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_id VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(14,2))
-- amounts in INR, txn_type CASH_DEP or CASH_WDL
questions.output_note: Rows in CTR_REPORT and NEAR_THRESHOLD after the insert, shown together. CT01 (exactly 10 lakh) goes only to CTR_REPORT because INSERT FIRST stops at the first true WHEN; with INSERT ALL it would also land in NEAR_THRESHOLD. CT05 is from 15-11-2026 and CT06 is below 9 lakh.
questions.task: In one statement, insert the 16-11-2026 cash transactions into CTR_REPORT (amount >= 1000000) or NEAR_THRESHOLD (amount >= 900000), so each row goes to at most one table.
questions.hint: Use INSERT FIRST with the 10 lakh WHEN clause written before the 9 lakh one.
questions.solution:
INSERT FIRST
  WHEN amount >= 1000000 THEN
    INTO ctr_report (txn_id, cust_id, amount)
    VALUES (txn_id, cust_id, amount)
  WHEN amount >= 900000 THEN
    INTO near_threshold (txn_id, cust_id, amount)
    VALUES (txn_id, cust_id, amount)
SELECT txn_id, cust_id, amount
FROM   cash_txn
WHERE  txn_date = DATE '2026-11-16';
questions.simple: Think of a post office sorting letters into cupboard drawers. Each letter is checked against rules from top to bottom: 'very big? put it in drawer 1', 'almost big? put it in drawer 2'. With INSERT FIRST, once a letter goes into a drawer, the sorter stops checking it. So a ₹10 lakh deposit goes only into the CTR drawer, not into both.
questions.remember: INSERT FIRST = first matching drawer only; ALL = every drawer.
questions.why: A multi-table insert reads the source query once and routes each row to one or more tables, which is faster and more consistent than separate INSERT ... SELECT statements. INSERT ALL evaluates every WHEN clause, so a row can go to several tables, while INSERT FIRST stops at the first true condition, so clause order matters. The whole statement is atomic, and an ELSE INTO branch can catch rows that match nothing.
questions.tip: To split one source into several targets I use a multi-table INSERT, choosing INSERT FIRST when each row must go to exactly one table.

questions.title: Life policies issued each year
questions.scenario: Kavita Menon in the life insurance operations team is preparing a board slide on business growth. She wants to know how many term policies were issued in each calendar year and the total sum assured.
questions.schema:
POLICY(policy_no VARCHAR2(10), holder_name VARCHAR2(50), plan_type VARCHAR2(20), issue_date DATE, sum_assured NUMBER(14,2))
-- issue_date is the day the policy started, sum_assured in INR
questions.task: Show each issue year, the number of policies and the total sum assured, oldest year first.
questions.hint: EXTRACT(YEAR FROM issue_date) gives just the year number; group by that same expression.
questions.solution:
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM issue_date) AS issue_year,
       COUNT(*)                       AS policies,
       SUM(sum_assured)               AS total_sum_assured
FROM   policy
GROUP  BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM issue_date)
ORDER  BY issue_year;
questions.simple: Think of a school register where each student has a full birthday like 31 December 2015. If you only look at the year, you can put everyone born in 2015 in one group. EXTRACT(YEAR FROM issue_date) picks out only the year from the date. GROUP BY then makes one group per year, and COUNT and SUM tell how many policies and how much money.
questions.remember: EXTRACT the year, then group by it.
questions.why: EXTRACT(YEAR FROM date) returns a NUMBER, so all dates in a calendar year collapse to one value and GROUP BY produces one row per year. The expression must be repeated in GROUP BY because Oracle 19c does not allow the SELECT alias there, although ORDER BY can use the alias. Note that 31-12-2025 and 01-01-2026 land in different groups, which is exactly what a calendar-year report needs.
questions.tip: For calendar-year totals I group by EXTRACT(YEAR FROM date); for financial-year reports in India I first shift the date with ADD_MONTHS(date, -3).

steps.say: Step one. EXTRACT YEAR pulls only the year out of the issue date.
COUNT star counts the policies, and SUM adds the sum assured.
Step two. GROUP BY the same year expression, so each year becomes one row.
Finally, ORDER BY issue year shows the oldest year first.

questions.title: Bonds by maturity, perpetuals last
questions.scenario: Deepak Agarwal on the treasury desk reviews the bank's bond holdings every morning. He wants the longest-dated bonds at the top, but perpetual bonds (which have no maturity date) must go to the bottom of the list, not the top.
questions.schema:
BOND_HOLDING(isin VARCHAR2(12), issuer VARCHAR2(40), face_value NUMBER(16,2), coupon_pct NUMBER(5,2), maturity_date DATE)
-- face_value in INR, maturity_date is NULL for perpetual bonds
questions.task: List isin, issuer and maturity_date with the latest maturity first and perpetual bonds (NULL maturity) at the end (ties by isin).
questions.hint: Add NULLS LAST after DESC, because Oracle puts NULLs first by default in a descending sort.
questions.simple: Imagine lining up friends from tallest to shortest, but two friends have not been measured yet. Oracle thinks an unknown height is 'bigger than everyone', so in a tallest-first line it puts them at the front. NULLS LAST tells Oracle: put the unknown ones at the back of the line. Here, perpetual bonds have no maturity date, so they go to the bottom.
questions.remember: DESC puts NULLs on top; add NULLS LAST.
questions.why: Oracle treats NULL as higher than any value when sorting, so ORDER BY ... ASC puts NULLs last and ORDER BY ... DESC puts NULLs first by default. NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST overrides that placement without changing the sort direction of real values. It is cleaner than tricks like NVL(maturity_date, DATE '1900-01-01'), which hide the intent.
questions.tip: I always state NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST explicitly in reports, because Oracle's default flips between ASC and DESC.

questions.title: RTGS settlement time SLA check
questions.scenario: Sunita Bhatt in payment operations must report RTGS payments that took more than 30 minutes to settle, as customers complain about high-value transfers. Some payments are still pending, and one crossed midnight because RTGS now runs 24x7.
questions.schema:
RTGS_TXN(utr VARCHAR2(22), sender_acct VARCHAR2(16), amount NUMBER(16,2), initiated_at DATE, settled_at DATE)
-- both columns have date and time, settled_at is NULL while pending, amount in INR
questions.task: For each payment show utr, amount, minutes taken and a status: 'PENDING' if not settled, 'DELAYED' if more than 30 minutes, otherwise 'ON TIME'.
questions.hint: Subtracting two DATEs gives days, so multiply by 24*60 to get minutes.
questions.solution:
SELECT utr,
       amount,
       ROUND((settled_at - initiated_at) * 24 * 60) AS mins_taken,
       CASE
         WHEN settled_at IS NULL THEN 'PENDING'
         WHEN (settled_at - initiated_at) * 24 * 60 > 30 THEN 'DELAYED'
         ELSE 'ON TIME'
       END AS sla_status
FROM   rtgs_txn
ORDER  BY utr;
questions.simple: Think of a stopwatch: you note the start time and the stop time, and the gap is how long the race took. In Oracle, stop date minus start date gives the gap in days, like 0.5 for half a day. Multiply by 24 to get hours and by 60 more to get minutes. If the stopwatch was never stopped (settled_at is empty), we call it PENDING instead of guessing.
questions.remember: Date minus date = days; times 1440 = minutes.
questions.why: DATE - DATE in Oracle returns a NUMBER of days including the fraction, so multiplying by 1440 converts it to minutes and naturally handles payments that cross midnight. When settled_at is NULL the difference is NULL, so the CASE checks IS NULL first; otherwise the NULL comparison would fall to ELSE and wrongly show 'ON TIME'. Exactly 30 minutes is not greater than 30, so UTR...0002 is on time.
questions.tip: For DATE columns I use (d2 - d1) * 1440 for minutes, and for TIMESTAMP columns I use EXTRACT on the INTERVAL result.

steps.say: Step one. Settled at minus initiated at gives days. Times twenty-four, times sixty, gives minutes.
Step two. CASE checks IS NULL first, so pending payments say PENDING.
If the minutes are more than thirty, the status is DELAYED.
Otherwise, it is ON TIME.

questions.title: Percentile of each fund in category
questions.scenario: Nikhil Saxena in the AMC's product team wants to tell distributors where each scheme stands within its SEBI category on 1-year returns. Two large-cap schemes have exactly the same return, and they must get the same percentile.
questions.schema:
FUND_RETURN(scheme_code VARCHAR2(10), scheme_name VARCHAR2(50), category VARCHAR2(20), return_1y NUMBER(6,2))
-- return_1y is the 1-year return in percent
questions.task: For each scheme show category, scheme_code, return_1y and its percentile within the category as a whole number (share of schemes in the category with the same or lower return), best return first within each category.
questions.hint: CUME_DIST() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY return_1y) returns a fraction between 0 and 1; multiply by 100 and ROUND.
questions.solution:
SELECT category,
       scheme_code,
       return_1y,
       ROUND(CUME_DIST() OVER (PARTITION BY category
                               ORDER BY return_1y) * 100) AS percentile
FROM   fund_return
ORDER  BY category, return_1y DESC, scheme_code;
questions.simple: Imagine your class gets test marks and you ask: how many kids scored the same as me or less? If 3 out of 4 kids did, you are at 75 percent. CUME_DIST does this count for each fund inside its own group (Large Cap or Mid Cap). Two funds with the same return are like two kids with the same marks, so they get the same answer.
questions.remember: CUME_DIST = share of rows at or below me.
questions.why: CUME_DIST computes (number of rows with value <= current value) / (rows in partition), so peers with equal ORDER BY values share the same result, here 75 for both 12.5% schemes. PERCENT_RANK instead computes (rank - 1) / (rows - 1) and starts at 0, so pick the one whose definition matches the business statement. PARTITION BY category keeps the comparison within each SEBI category.
questions.tip: For 'top X percent' questions I use CUME_DIST or PERCENT_RANK and explain how each treats ties, instead of hand-coding counts.

questions.title: Mark NPAs and audit in bulk
questions.scenario: Prakash Kulkarni runs the month-end NPA job for the MSME loan book. Loans that are more than 90 days past due must become NPA with a 15% provision, and the exact loans and provisions changed must go into an audit table without a second query on LOAN_ACCT.
questions.schema:
LOAN_ACCT(loan_id VARCHAR2(10), borrower VARCHAR2(50), outstanding NUMBER(14,2), dpd NUMBER, status VARCHAR2(5), provision NUMBER(14,2))
-- status STD or NPA, dpd = days past due, amounts in INR
NPA_AUDIT(loan_id VARCHAR2(10), provision NUMBER(14,2), marked_on DATE)
-- one row per loan newly marked NPA
questions.output_note: NPA_AUDIT after the block. LOAN_ACCT now shows L201 and L203 as NPA with provisions 180000 and 64500; L202 (exactly 90 dpd) stays STD and L205 was already NPA. DBMS_OUTPUT prints '2 loans marked NPA'.
questions.task: Write an anonymous block that marks STD loans with dpd > 90 as NPA with provision = ROUND(outstanding * 0.15), captures the changed loan_ids and provisions with RETURNING BULK COLLECT, inserts them into NPA_AUDIT with FORALL dated 19-11-2026, and commits.
questions.hint: Put RETURNING loan_id, provision BULK COLLECT INTO two nested tables at the end of the UPDATE, then FORALL over 1 .. l_ids.COUNT.
questions.simple: Think of a teacher who stamps 'late' on some homework and, while stamping, writes each name on a list. She does not walk around the class a second time to find who got stamped. RETURNING ... BULK COLLECT is that list: the UPDATE changes the rows and hands back their ids and new values in one go. FORALL then writes the whole list into the audit table in one trip.
questions.remember: Change rows and catch what changed in one trip.
questions.why: RETURNING ... BULK COLLECT INTO fills collections with the post-update values of every affected row, so there is no re-query and no risk of picking up rows changed by another session in between. FORALL sends all audit inserts to the SQL engine in one context switch, and with an empty collection the 1 .. 0 range simply does nothing. The returned provision is the new value (180000 and 64500), and dpd = 90 is not > 90, so L202 stays standard.
questions.tip: When I need the keys or new values of rows I just updated, I use RETURNING BULK COLLECT INTO instead of a second SELECT, then FORALL for the follow-up DML.

steps.say: Step one. We declare two collections, to hold loan ids and provisions.
Step two. The UPDATE marks overdue standard loans as N.P.A. and sets a fifteen percent provision.
RETURNING BULK COLLECT hands back the changed ids and provisions in one go.
Step three. FORALL inserts the whole list into the audit table in one trip.
Finally, we print the count and commit.

questions.title: Split legacy KYC document lists
questions.scenario: Ritu Chawla is migrating KYC data from a legacy core banking system where all documents a customer submitted are stored in one comma-separated column. The new KYC table needs one row per document, and some lists have spaces after commas or are empty.
questions.schema:
LEGACY_KYC(cust_id VARCHAR2(10), cust_name VARCHAR2(50), doc_list VARCHAR2(200))
-- doc_list like 'PAN,AADHAAR'; NULL when no document was captured
questions.task: Return cust_id, doc_seq (position in the list) and doc_type (trimmed) with one row per document, skipping customers with no list, ordered by cust_id and doc_seq.
questions.hint: Use CROSS APPLY with a CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(doc_list, ',') + 1 row generator, and REGEXP_SUBSTR(doc_list, '[^,]+', 1, level) to pick each piece.
questions.solution:
SELECT k.cust_id,
       d.doc_seq,
       TRIM(REGEXP_SUBSTR(k.doc_list, '[^,]+', 1, d.doc_seq)) AS doc_type
FROM   legacy_kyc k
CROSS  APPLY (SELECT LEVEL AS doc_seq
              FROM   dual
              CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(k.doc_list, ',') + 1) d
WHERE  k.doc_list IS NOT NULL
ORDER  BY k.cust_id, d.doc_seq;
questions.simple: Imagine a shopping bill where someone wrote 'milk, bread, eggs' on one line, and you need each item on its own line. First you count the commas to know how many items there are (2 commas = 3 items). Then you make that many numbered lines and pick item 1, item 2, item 3. TRIM removes the extra spaces. If the line is empty, there is nothing to copy.
questions.remember: Count commas plus one, then pick piece number LEVEL.
questions.why: REGEXP_COUNT(doc_list, ',') + 1 gives the number of elements, and the correlated CROSS APPLY runs a CONNECT BY LEVEL generator per customer, avoiding the classic cross-row explosion of a plain CONNECT BY over a multi-row table. CONNECT BY always returns the root row even when LEVEL <= NULL is false, so a NULL list would produce one NULL document unless filtered with doc_list IS NOT NULL. REGEXP_SUBSTR with '[^,]+' and occurrence = doc_seq extracts each piece, and TRIM cleans the leading spaces.
questions.tip: To split delimited strings per row in 19c I use CROSS APPLY with CONNECT BY LEVEL, or a PRIOR SYS_GUID() trick in older versions, so rows do not multiply across customers.

questions.title: Match card authorisations to settlements
questions.scenario: Harish Reddy reconciles debit card authorisations with the scheme settlement file every day. A customer often has two authorisations of the same amount (two Rs 250 metro top-ups) but only one has settled, so a simple join on card and amount double-matches.
questions.schema:
CARD_AUTH(auth_id VARCHAR2(10), card_no VARCHAR2(16), amount NUMBER(12,2), auth_time DATE)
-- card_no is masked, amount in INR, auth_time has date and time
CARD_SETTLE(settle_id VARCHAR2(10), card_no VARCHAR2(16), amount NUMBER(12,2), settle_date DATE)
-- one row per settled transaction from the card scheme
questions.task: Pair the 1st authorisation of a card and amount with the 1st settlement of that card and amount, the 2nd with the 2nd, and so on (oldest first). Show card_no, amount, auth_id, settle_id and recon_status MATCHED, AUTH ONLY or SETTLE ONLY.
questions.hint: Number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY card_no, amount ORDER BY time) on both sides, then FULL OUTER JOIN on card_no, amount and that number.
questions.solution:
WITH a AS (
  SELECT auth_id, card_no, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY card_no, amount
                            ORDER BY auth_time, auth_id) AS rn
  FROM   card_auth
), s AS (
  SELECT settle_id, card_no, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY card_no, amount
                            ORDER BY settle_date, settle_id) AS rn
  FROM   card_settle
)
SELECT COALESCE(a.card_no, s.card_no) AS card_no,
       COALESCE(a.amount,  s.amount)  AS amount,
       a.auth_id,
       s.settle_id,
       CASE
         WHEN a.auth_id IS NULL   THEN 'SETTLE ONLY'
         WHEN s.settle_id IS NULL THEN 'AUTH ONLY'
         ELSE 'MATCHED'
       END AS recon_status
FROM   a
FULL   OUTER JOIN s
       ON  s.card_no = a.card_no
       AND s.amount  = a.amount
       AND s.rn      = a.rn
ORDER  BY 1, 2, COALESCE(a.rn, s.rn);
questions.simple: Think of a school dance where boys and girls with the same shirt colour must pair up. If there are two red-shirt boys but one red-shirt girl, both boys cannot dance with her. So you number them: red boy 1 dances with red girl 1, and red boy 2 waits alone. ROW_NUMBER gives each row its number inside its group (same card, same amount). Then we join on that number too, so nobody is matched twice.
questions.remember: Number each side, then join on the number too.
questions.why: Joining only on card_no and amount is a many-to-many join, so one settlement would match both Rs 250 authorisations and look fully reconciled. Adding ROW_NUMBER per (card_no, amount) ordered by time turns duplicates into distinct keys, giving one-to-one pairs in FIFO order. The FULL OUTER JOIN then exposes both sides' leftovers: A2 and A5 are unsettled authorisations and S4 is a settlement without an authorisation (for example a force post).
questions.tip: When reconciling records with duplicate keys I add ROW_NUMBER per key on both sides and join on it, so matches are one-to-one and leftovers show up in a FULL OUTER JOIN.

questions.title: Savings interest on tiered rate slabs
questions.scenario: Meera Krishnan in the deposits product team is testing a new savings scheme where each part of the balance earns its own rate: up to Rs 1 lakh at 2.7%, the next Rs 4 lakh at 3%, and anything above Rs 5 lakh at 3.5%. She wants the yearly interest and effective rate per account from the slab table, not hard-coded numbers.
questions.schema:
SB_BALANCE(acct_no VARCHAR2(12), cust_name VARCHAR2(50), eod_balance NUMBER(14,2))
-- end-of-day balance in INR
RATE_SLAB(slab_from NUMBER(14,2), slab_to NUMBER(14,2), rate_pct NUMBER(5,2))
-- balance portion above slab_from up to slab_to earns rate_pct; slab_to NULL = no upper limit
questions.task: For each account show acct_no, eod_balance, annual_interest (sum over slabs of the balance portion in that slab times its rate) and effective_rate = interest * 100 / balance rounded to 2 decimals, assuming the balance stays the same for a year.
questions.hint: Join each account to every slab whose slab_from is below the balance, and take LEAST(balance, NVL(slab_to, balance)) - slab_from as the portion in that slab.
questions.solution:
SELECT a.acct_no,
       a.eod_balance,
       SUM((LEAST(a.eod_balance, NVL(s.slab_to, a.eod_balance)) - s.slab_from)
           * s.rate_pct / 100) AS annual_interest,
       ROUND(SUM((LEAST(a.eod_balance, NVL(s.slab_to, a.eod_balance)) - s.slab_from)
           * s.rate_pct / 100) * 100 / a.eod_balance, 2) AS effective_rate
FROM   sb_balance a
JOIN   rate_slab  s
       ON a.eod_balance > s.slab_from
GROUP  BY a.acct_no, a.eod_balance
ORDER  BY a.acct_no;
questions.simple: Think of a staircase of cupboard drawers: the first drawer holds up to Rs 1 lakh, the second holds the next Rs 4 lakh, and the top drawer holds the rest. You fill drawers from the bottom, and each drawer pays its own interest rate. For every drawer we work out how much money is inside it and multiply by its rate. Adding the drawers gives the total interest.
questions.remember: Fill slabs bottom up; each slab pays only its part.
questions.why: The join condition eod_balance > slab_from attaches only the slabs the balance actually reaches, and LEAST(balance, NVL(slab_to, balance)) - slab_from caps the portion at the slab width, with NVL handling the open-ended top slab. Summing portion * rate after GROUP BY gives the marginal (tiered) interest, which differs from applying one rate to the whole balance: Rs 12 lakh earns 39200, an effective 3.27%, not 3.5%. Keeping slabs in a table means a rate change is a data update, not a code release.
questions.tip: For slab-based interest, TDS or charges I join to a slab table and use LEAST/GREATEST to cap each portion, so rate changes need no code change.

questions.title: Catch accidental duplicate UPI payments
questions.scenario: Customers of a payments bank complain that a slow app made them pay the same shop twice. The fraud team, led by Kavita Rao, wants to list every payment that repeats an earlier one: same payer, same payee and same amount within 10 minutes.
questions.schema:
UPI_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(10), payer_vpa VARCHAR2(40), payee_vpa VARCHAR2(40), amount NUMBER(12,2), txn_time DATE)
-- txn_time has date and time, amount in INR
questions.output_note: T03 came 26 minutes after T02, and T05 has a different amount, so they are not repeats. T07 is exactly 10 minutes, which counts.
questions.task: List each repeated payment: txn_id, payer_vpa, amount and the minutes since the previous identical payment (same payer, payee and amount), when that gap is 10 minutes or less.
questions.hint: LAG with PARTITION BY payer, payee and amount gives the previous identical payment's time.
questions.solution:
SELECT txn_id, payer_vpa, amount,
       ROUND((txn_time - prev_time) * 1440) AS mins_gap
FROM (
  SELECT t.*,
         LAG(txn_time) OVER (
           PARTITION BY payer_vpa, payee_vpa, amount
           ORDER BY txn_time) AS prev_time
  FROM upi_txn t
)
WHERE (txn_time - prev_time) * 1440 <= 10
ORDER BY txn_id;
questions.simple: Imagine every payment stands in a queue with its twins: same payer, same shop, same amount. Each payment looks at the twin just before it in the queue. If that twin paid less than 10 minutes earlier, this payment is a repeat. LAG is how a row looks at the row just before it.
questions.remember: LAG looks one row back inside each PARTITION.
questions.why: LAG(txn_time) OVER (PARTITION BY payer_vpa, payee_vpa, amount ORDER BY txn_time) returns the previous identical payment's time, NULL for the first one. The gap in days times 1440 gives minutes. The filter must be in an outer query because window functions cannot be used in WHERE. The first payment of each group has NULL prev_time and drops out automatically.
questions.tip: Window functions run after WHERE, so I filter on them in an outer query or a CTE.

steps.say: Step one. Inside, LAG looks at the previous payment's time.
PARTITION BY makes groups of twins: same payer, same payee, same amount.
ORDER BY time, so the previous row really is the earlier payment.
Step two. Outside, keep only rows where the gap is ten minutes or less. Days times fourteen forty gives minutes.
We filter outside, because window functions are not allowed in WHERE.

questions.title: Find mid-size SIP mandates
questions.scenario: Ritu Sharma at an AMC is launching a reminder campaign for mid-size SIP investors. She wants every SIP whose monthly amount is from 1,000 to 5,000 INR, both ends included.
questions.schema:
SIP_MANDATE(sip_id VARCHAR2(5), investor VARCHAR2(30), fund VARCHAR2(30), monthly_amt NUMBER(12,2))
-- monthly_amt in INR
questions.output_note: S2 (exactly 1,000) and S4 (exactly 5,000) are included because BETWEEN includes both ends.
questions.task: Show sip_id, investor and monthly_amt for SIPs with monthly_amt from 1,000 to 5,000 inclusive, smallest amount first.
questions.hint: BETWEEN low AND high includes both low and high.
questions.solution:
SELECT sip_id, investor, monthly_amt
FROM sip_mandate
WHERE monthly_amt BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000
ORDER BY monthly_amt;
questions.simple: Think of a ride at a fair that allows kids from 100 cm to 150 cm tall. A kid who is exactly 100 cm or exactly 150 cm can still ride. BETWEEN works the same way: it keeps values from the low number to the high number, including both edges.
questions.remember: BETWEEN keeps both edges: low and high are in.
questions.why: monthly_amt BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000 is the same as monthly_amt >= 1000 AND monthly_amt <= 5000. The low value must come first; BETWEEN 5000 AND 1000 returns no rows. ORDER BY monthly_amt sorts ascending by default.
questions.tip: BETWEEN is inclusive on both sides, so for dates with time I prefer >= start AND < next day.

steps.say: Step one. Pick the three columns we want to show.
Step two. BETWEEN keeps amounts from one thousand to five thousand, and both edges count.
Finally, sort from the smallest amount to the biggest.

questions.title: Loans with no November EMI
questions.scenario: Sandeep Nair in the retail loans team must call borrowers whose November EMI has not arrived. The November payments file is loaded into its own table.
questions.schema:
LOAN(loan_id VARCHAR2(5), borrower VARCHAR2(30), emi_amt NUMBER(10))
EMI_PAYMENT_NOV(pay_id VARCHAR2(5), loan_id VARCHAR2(5), pay_date DATE, amount NUMBER(10))
-- one row per payment received in November, amounts in INR
questions.output_note: L103 paid twice but still appears only in the matched side, so it is not listed.
questions.task: List loan_id, borrower and emi_amt of loans that have no row in EMI_PAYMENT_NOV, ordered by loan_id.
questions.hint: LEFT JOIN the payments and keep rows where the payment side is NULL.
questions.solution:
SELECT l.loan_id, l.borrower, l.emi_amt
FROM loan l
LEFT JOIN emi_payment_nov p ON p.loan_id = l.loan_id
WHERE p.pay_id IS NULL
ORDER BY l.loan_id;
questions.simple: Imagine a class register and a pile of homework sheets. You put each sheet next to the student's name. The names with an empty space next to them did not hand in homework. LEFT JOIN keeps every loan, and IS NULL picks the loans with nothing next to them.
questions.remember: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL = who is missing.
questions.why: LEFT JOIN keeps every LOAN row and fills payment columns with NULL when no match exists. Filtering WHERE p.pay_id IS NULL keeps only unmatched loans. Test a NOT NULL column of the right table, such as its key, so a real NULL value is not mistaken for a missing row.
questions.tip: For 'rows with no match' I use LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL or NOT EXISTS, never NOT IN on a nullable column.

steps.say: Step one. Start from the loan table, so every loan is in the list.
Step two. LEFT JOIN the November payments. Loans with no payment get empty payment columns.
Finally, keep only rows where the payment is empty. Those borrowers have not paid.

questions.title: First and latest balance per account
questions.scenario: Anjali Menon, a branch manager, reviews savings accounts for November. For each account she wants the balance after its first transaction and after its latest transaction. Rows were loaded out of time order.
questions.schema:
ACCT_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(5), acct_no VARCHAR2(10), txn_time DATE, balance_after NUMBER(12))
-- txn_time has date and time, balance in INR
questions.output_note: For SB2002, X6 has the highest txn_id but happened earlier (09:10) than X5 (14:30), so the latest balance is 15,500.
questions.task: For each acct_no show first_bal (balance_after of the earliest txn_time) and last_bal (balance_after of the latest txn_time), one row per account.
questions.hint: FIRST_VALUE ordered DESC gives the last row without worrying about the window frame.
questions.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT acct_no,
       FIRST_VALUE(balance_after) OVER (
         PARTITION BY acct_no ORDER BY txn_time) AS first_bal,
       FIRST_VALUE(balance_after) OVER (
         PARTITION BY acct_no ORDER BY txn_time DESC) AS last_bal
FROM acct_txn
ORDER BY acct_no;
questions.simple: Think of a passbook where each line shows the balance after that entry. The first line shows where the month started and the last line shows where it is now. FIRST_VALUE reads the top line. If we flip the passbook upside down, FIRST_VALUE reads the latest line instead.
questions.remember: Latest value? FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY DESC.
questions.why: FIRST_VALUE returns the first row of the ordered partition, which is safe with the default frame. LAST_VALUE with ORDER BY uses the frame ending at the current row, so it would just return the current row's value. Ordering DESC and taking FIRST_VALUE avoids that trap, and DISTINCT collapses the repeated rows to one per account.
questions.tip: I avoid LAST_VALUE with the default frame; FIRST_VALUE with reversed ORDER BY gives the latest value safely.

steps.say: Step one. FIRST_VALUE, ordered by time, reads the balance of the earliest transaction for each account.
steps.to: PARTITION BY acct_no ORDER BY txn_time) AS first_bal

steps.say: Step two. Same function, but ordered newest first. Now the first row is the latest transaction.
steps.find: PARTITION BY acct_no ORDER BY txn_time DESC

steps.say: Finally, DISTINCT squeezes the repeated rows into one row per account.

questions.title: Countries each customer remitted to
questions.scenario: Under the RBI Liberalised Remittance Scheme, compliance officer Harish Kulkarni reviews outward remittances. For each customer he wants the number of remittances and a clean, alphabetical list of destination countries without repeats.
questions.schema:
OUTWARD_REMIT(remit_id VARCHAR2(5), cust_id VARCHAR2(5), country VARCHAR2(20), amount_inr NUMBER(12))
-- country may be NULL when not yet captured
questions.output_note: USA appears once for C11 thanks to DISTINCT. C12's NULL country is skipped by LISTAGG but still counted by COUNT(*).
questions.task: For each cust_id show remit_cnt (all remittances) and countries: distinct countries joined with ', ' in alphabetical order.
questions.hint: Oracle 19c allows LISTAGG(DISTINCT col, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col).
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id,
       COUNT(*) AS remit_cnt,
       LISTAGG(DISTINCT country, ', ')
         WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY country) AS countries
FROM outward_remit
GROUP BY cust_id
ORDER BY cust_id;
questions.simple: Imagine writing the names of places you sent postcards to. If you sent two to the USA, you still write USA only once, in A to Z order. LISTAGG glues the names into one line, and DISTINCT stops repeats. Blank names are simply left out.
questions.remember: LISTAGG glues rows into one string; DISTINCT drops repeats.
questions.why: LISTAGG concatenates values of a group into one string in the WITHIN GROUP order. Since 19c, DISTINCT removes duplicate values inside the list; before that you needed a subquery with DISTINCT or ROW_NUMBER. NULL values are ignored by LISTAGG, while COUNT(*) still counts that row.
questions.tip: On 19c I use LISTAGG(DISTINCT ...), and ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE when the list might exceed 4000 bytes.

steps.say: Step one. Group the rows by customer.
Step two. COUNT star counts every remittance, even one with a blank country.
Finally, LISTAGG DISTINCT glues each country once, sorted A to Z, with a comma between.
steps.to: WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY country) AS countries

questions.title: Mobile banking users retained each month
questions.scenario: Deepa Iyer, head of digital banking, tracks how many app users keep coming back. A user is retained in a month if they also logged in during the previous calendar month.
questions.schema:
APP_LOGIN(cust_id VARCHAR2(5), login_time DATE)
-- one row per login, time included; many logins per month possible
questions.output_note: October: U1 and U5 were also active in September. November: U1 and U3; U2 skipped October, so it does not count. September has no earlier month in the data, so it has no row.
questions.task: For each month, count distinct users who logged in that month and also in the previous calendar month. Show login_month as YYYY-MM.
questions.hint: Compare TRUNC(login_time,'MM') of the inner row with ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(outer login_time,'MM'), -1).
questions.solution:
SELECT TO_CHAR(TRUNC(n.login_time, 'MM'), 'YYYY-MM') AS login_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT n.cust_id) AS retained_users
FROM app_login n
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM app_login o
  WHERE o.cust_id = n.cust_id
    AND TRUNC(o.login_time, 'MM') = ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(n.login_time, 'MM'), -1))
GROUP BY TRUNC(n.login_time, 'MM')
ORDER BY login_month;
questions.simple: Think of a gym that wants to know who came back. A member counts as 'back' in November only if they also came in October. For each login, the query checks last month's list for the same person. Then it counts each person once per month.
questions.remember: Retained = here this month AND here last month.
questions.why: TRUNC(date,'MM') maps every login to the first day of its month, and ADD_MONTHS(...,-1) gives the previous calendar month, so September to November gaps do not count. EXISTS stops at the first matching earlier login. COUNT(DISTINCT cust_id) is needed because one user can log in many times a month.
questions.tip: For retention I bucket by TRUNC(date,'MM') and use EXISTS or a self-join on month minus one, counting DISTINCT users.

steps.say: Step one. Look at every login and turn its date into a month.
Step two. EXISTS checks whether the same customer also logged in during the month just before.
Step three. Group by month.
Finally, count each customer once, because one person can log in many times.

questions.title: Block only high-risk cards in bulk
questions.scenario: Card fraud lead Rakesh Bhatia gets risk alerts every hour. Only cards with a risk score of 80 or more must be blocked, using one bulk update.
questions.schema:
CARD(card_no VARCHAR2(5), holder VARCHAR2(20), status VARCHAR2(10))
FRAUD_ALERT(alert_id VARCHAR2(5), card_no VARCHAR2(5), risk_score NUMBER(3))
-- risk_score 0-100
questions.output_note: CARD table after the block runs; it prints 'Blocked: 2'. With FORALL i IN 1 .. l_alerts.COUNT instead, it would fail with ORA-22160 because elements 2 and 4 were deleted.
questions.task: Load all alerts into a collection, delete the ones below 80, then block the remaining cards with a single FORALL and print how many were blocked.
questions.hint: After DELETE the collection has gaps; FORALL i IN INDICES OF skips them.
questions.simple: Imagine a row of numbered lockers, and you empty lockers 2 and 4. If you walk past every number and open each one, you get stuck at the empty ones. INDICES OF only visits lockers that still have something inside. That is how FORALL skips the deleted alerts.
questions.remember: Gaps in the collection? FORALL ... INDICES OF.
questions.why: DELETE(i) on a nested table leaves gaps, so the collection becomes sparse. FORALL i IN 1..COUNT would hit a deleted index and raise ORA-22160, while INDICES OF binds only existing elements in one context switch. After FORALL, SQL%ROWCOUNT holds the total rows changed by all executions.
questions.tip: For sparse collections I use FORALL INDICES OF, or VALUES OF when a second collection holds the positions to process.

steps.say: Step one. Load every fraud alert into a collection in one go.
Step two. Delete alerts with a score below eighty. This leaves holes in the collection.
Step three. FORALL with INDICES OF skips the holes and blocks the remaining cards in one bulk call.
steps.find: FORALL i IN INDICES OF l_alerts

steps.say: Finally, print how many cards were blocked, and commit.

questions.title: Peak simultaneous calls at card helpline
questions.scenario: Nisha Verma plans staffing for the credit card helpline. She needs the highest number of calls running at the same moment and when it first happened. A call ending at 10:05 does not overlap one starting at 10:05.
questions.schema:
CALL_LOG(call_id VARCHAR2(5), agent_id VARCHAR2(5), start_time DATE, end_time DATE)
-- times with minutes; end_time > start_time
questions.output_note: At 10:05 K1 ends before K3 starts, so the count stays at 2. Without ordering ends first, 10:05 would wrongly show 3.
questions.task: Return peak_time and peak_calls: the maximum number of calls in progress at once and the earliest time it was reached.
questions.hint: Turn each call into a +1 at start and a -1 at end, then take a running SUM ordered by time, with -1 before +1 on ties.
questions.solution:
WITH ev AS (
  SELECT start_time AS t, 1 AS chg FROM call_log
  UNION ALL
  SELECT end_time, -1 FROM call_log
), run AS (
  SELECT t, SUM(chg) OVER (ORDER BY t, chg
           ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS live
  FROM ev
)
SELECT t AS peak_time, live AS peak_calls
FROM run
ORDER BY live DESC, t
FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY;
questions.simple: Think of a room with a door counter. Every time someone walks in, add one; when someone walks out, take one away. The biggest number the counter ever shows is the busiest moment. If one person leaves exactly as another enters, we count the leaver first.
questions.remember: Start = +1, end = -1, running sum = people inside.
questions.why: Each call becomes two events, and a running SUM of +1/-1 ordered by time gives the number of live calls after each event. Ordering by t, chg puts -1 before +1 at the same instant, so touching intervals do not overlap. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING makes tied timestamps accumulate one event at a time instead of all together as RANGE would.
questions.tip: For max concurrency I unpivot intervals into +1/-1 events and take a running sum; the tie order decides whether touching intervals overlap.

steps.say: Step one. Turn each call into two events: plus one when it starts, minus one when it ends.
steps.find: SELECT start_time AS t, 1 AS chg

steps.say: Step two. A running sum in time order counts the calls live after each event. Ends come before starts on a tie.
Finally, sort by the biggest count, earliest time first, and keep the top row.

questions.title: Average buy price after each trade
questions.scenario: Broker analyst Karan Malhotra shows clients their average buy price for a share. Buys change the average; sells reduce quantity but keep the average the same.
questions.schema:
TRADE(trade_no VARCHAR2(5), client_id VARCHAR2(6), side CHAR(1), qty NUMBER(8), price NUMBER(10,2), trade_time DATE)
-- side B = buy, S = sell; one share, one client; price in INR; first trade is a buy
questions.output_note: TR4: (90 x 210 + 30 x 190) / 120 = 205. After TR5 the holding is 0, so TR6 starts a fresh average of 300.
questions.task: In trade_time order, show trade_no, side, hold_qty and avg_cost (2 decimals) after each trade. Buy: weighted average of old holding and new buy. Sell: average unchanged.
questions.hint: Each row depends on the previous row's result, so use recursive WITH joined on row number + 1.
questions.solution:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT tr.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY trade_time) AS rn
  FROM trade tr
), r (rn, trade_no, side, hold_qty, avg_cost) AS (
  SELECT rn, trade_no, side, qty, price FROM t WHERE rn = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.rn, t.trade_no, t.side,
         CASE t.side WHEN 'B' THEN r.hold_qty + t.qty
                     ELSE r.hold_qty - t.qty END,
         CASE t.side WHEN 'B'
              THEN ROUND((r.hold_qty * r.avg_cost + t.qty * t.price)
                         / (r.hold_qty + t.qty), 2)
              ELSE r.avg_cost END
  FROM r JOIN t ON t.rn = r.rn + 1
)
SELECT trade_no, side, hold_qty, avg_cost
FROM r
ORDER BY rn;
