questions.simple: Imagine a jar of marbles bought at different prices. When you add marbles, the average price per marble changes. When you give some away, the average stays the same, there are just fewer marbles. The query walks through trades one by one, carrying the jar's count and average forward.
questions.remember: Recursive WITH = carry yesterday's answer into today's row.
questions.why: A weighted average cost depends on the previous row's computed values, which a plain window SUM cannot express once sells are mixed in. Recursive WITH seeds the first trade and joins each new trade on rn = previous rn + 1, carrying hold_qty and avg_cost forward. Oracle requires the column alias list on a recursive subquery factoring clause.
questions.tip: When each row needs the previous row's computed result, not just its raw value, I use recursive WITH or MODEL instead of LAG.

steps.say: Step one. Number the trades in time order.
steps.find: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY trade_time) AS rn

steps.say: Step two. The anchor: the first trade sets the holding and the average price.
steps.find: SELECT rn, trade_no, side, qty, price FROM t WHERE rn = 1

steps.say: Step three. Each next trade joins to the previous result. Buys add quantity, sells take it away.
steps.find: CASE t.side WHEN 'B' THEN r.hold_qty + t.qty
steps.to: FROM r JOIN t ON t.rn = r.rn + 1

steps.say: Finally, for a buy, the new average mixes old and new cost. For a sell, the average stays.

questions.title: Customers holding a gold loan
questions.scenario: Sunita Rao, gold loan desk head at a Pune branch, wants to call every customer who has a gold loan. Some customers have more than one gold loan.
questions.schema:
CUSTOMER(cust_id VARCHAR2(5), cust_name VARCHAR2(30), city VARCHAR2(20))
LOAN(loan_id VARCHAR2(5), cust_id VARCHAR2(5), loan_type VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- loan_type: GOLD, HOME, PERSONAL; amount in INR
questions.output_note: Chetan has two gold loans but appears once, because IN only checks membership.
questions.task: List cust_id and cust_name of customers who have at least one GOLD loan, each customer once, ordered by cust_id.
questions.hint: Put the gold-loan customer ids in a subquery and filter with IN.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, cust_name
FROM customer
WHERE cust_id IN (SELECT cust_id
                  FROM loan
                  WHERE loan_type = 'GOLD')
ORDER BY cust_id;
questions.simple: Think of a teacher with a list of children who brought a lunch box. She reads the class register and ticks a name if it is on that list. Even if a child brought two lunch boxes, the name is ticked once. The subquery makes the list, and IN checks each customer against it.
questions.remember: IN = "is this name on the list?"
questions.why: The subquery returns the set of cust_id values with a GOLD loan, and IN keeps each CUSTOMER row whose cust_id is in that set. Because the filter is on the outer table, duplicates in LOAN do not multiply rows, unlike an INNER JOIN. Oracle typically turns this into a semi-join.
questions.tip: When I only need to check existence in another table, I use IN or EXISTS instead of a join, so I never get duplicate rows.

steps.say: Step one. The inner query lists every customer id that has a gold loan.
Step two. The outer query keeps a customer only if their id is on that list. Chetan shows once, not twice.
Finally, sort the result by customer id.

questions.title: UPI count by app and status
questions.scenario: Rahul Iyer from the UPI operations team wants a quick daily summary. For each UPI app, how many payments succeeded or failed, and for how much.
questions.schema:
UPI_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(5), app_name VARCHAR2(15), status VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- status: SUCCESS or FAILED; amount in INR
questions.task: Show app_name, status, the number of payments (txn_count) and their total amount (total_amt) for every app and status pair, ordered by app_name then status.
questions.hint: List both columns in GROUP BY, so each app-and-status pair becomes one group.
questions.solution:
SELECT app_name, status,
       COUNT(*)    AS txn_count,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amt
FROM upi_txn
GROUP BY app_name, status
ORDER BY app_name, status;
questions.simple: Imagine sorting coins into boxes, one box for each colour and size together, like 'big gold' and 'small gold'. Then you count the coins in each box and add up their value. GROUP BY with two columns makes one box for every app and status pair, then COUNT and SUM work inside each box.
questions.remember: Two columns in GROUP BY = one row per pair.
questions.why: GROUP BY app_name, status forms one group per distinct combination of the two columns. COUNT(*) and SUM(amount) are then computed separately inside each group. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must appear in the GROUP BY, or Oracle raises ORA-00979.
questions.tip: Every column I select that is not inside an aggregate must also be in GROUP BY.

steps.say: Step one. Group the payments by app and status together, so each pair becomes one box.
Step two. Inside each box, count the payments and add up the amounts.
Finally, sort by app name and then status.

questions.concept: Latest row per key with tie-break
questions.title: Current status of each motor policy
questions.scenario: Meera Pillai in motor insurance servicing needs today's status of each policy. A policy can get two status changes on the same day, so the date alone cannot decide.
questions.schema:
POLICY_STATUS(policy_no VARCHAR2(5), status VARCHAR2(12), status_date DATE, seq_no NUMBER(6))
-- one row per status change; seq_no always increases, so a higher seq_no is the later change
questions.output_note: MP1 lapsed and was revived on the same day; seq_no 3 breaks the tie, so REVIVED wins.
questions.task: Show policy_no, status and status_date of the latest status per policy. Latest means the highest status_date; on the same date, the highest seq_no. Order by policy_no.
questions.hint: Use ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY policy_no and ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC, then keep row 1.
questions.solution:
SELECT policy_no, status, status_date
FROM (
  SELECT ps.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY policy_no
                            ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC) AS rn
  FROM policy_status ps
)
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY policy_no;
questions.simple: Think of a diary where you write what happened each day, and some days have two entries. To know the latest news, you open the last page and read the bottom entry. ROW_NUMBER numbers each policy's entries from newest to oldest, using the entry number to break same-day ties, and we keep entry number 1.
questions.remember: Latest per group = ROW_NUMBER, newest first, keep 1.
questions.why: ROW_NUMBER restarts at 1 for each policy_no and orders rows by status_date DESC, then seq_no DESC, so the tie on 10-09-2026 is resolved deterministically. Filtering rn = 1 must happen in an outer query because window functions cannot appear in WHERE. Without the seq_no tie-breaker, Oracle could return LAPSED or REVIVED for MP1 on different runs.
questions.tip: I always add a unique tie-breaker column to ROW_NUMBER's ORDER BY, otherwise "latest" is not deterministic.

steps.say: Step one. For each policy, number the status rows from newest to oldest.
steps.to: ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC) AS rn

steps.say: Step two. On the same date, the higher sequence number counts as later. That makes revived beat lapsed.
steps.find: ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC) AS rn

steps.say: Finally, keep only row number one, the current status of each policy.

questions.title: Average CIBIL score by branch
questions.scenario: Credit manager Arjun Bhatia compares applicant quality across branches. New-to-credit applicants have no CIBIL score, stored as NULL, and must not drag the average down.
questions.schema:
BUREAU_SCORE(app_id VARCHAR2(5), branch VARCHAR2(15), cibil_score NUMBER(3))
-- cibil_score is NULL for new-to-credit (NTC) applicants
questions.output_note: Indore averages (760 + 700) / 2 = 730, not 1460 / 3. Nashik has only NULL scores, so its average is NULL.
questions.task: Per branch, show applicants (all rows), avg_score (average of scores rounded to a whole number, ignoring NTC) and ntc_count (applicants with no score). Order by branch.
questions.hint: AVG already skips NULLs; NTC count is COUNT(*) minus COUNT(cibil_score).
questions.solution:
SELECT branch,
       COUNT(*)                       AS applicants,
       ROUND(AVG(cibil_score))        AS avg_score,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(cibil_score)  AS ntc_count
FROM bureau_score
GROUP BY branch
ORDER BY branch;
questions.simple: Imagine three friends in a race, but one did not run. To find the average time, you only add the two who ran and divide by two. AVG does the same: blank scores are left out completely. If nobody in a branch has a score, the average is blank too.
questions.remember: AVG skips NULLs: they are not zero.
questions.why: Aggregate functions except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs, so AVG(cibil_score) divides by COUNT(cibil_score), not COUNT(*). A group with only NULLs returns NULL from AVG, as Nashik shows. Using AVG(NVL(cibil_score, 0)) would wrongly count NTC applicants as score 0.
questions.tip: I check whether a NULL should mean "unknown" or "zero" before averaging; AVG treats it as unknown and skips it.

steps.say: Step one. Count every applicant in the branch, with or without a score.
Step two. Average the scores. Blank scores are skipped, so Indore is seven sixty plus seven hundred, divided by two.
Finally, all rows minus scored rows gives the new-to-credit count.

questions.title: Reject RTGS requests below minimum
questions.scenario: Payments lead Kavita Menon loads RTGS requests in a batch. RTGS needs at least INR 2 lakh, enforced by a CHECK constraint. Bad rows must be logged, not stop the batch.
questions.schema:
RTGS_REQUEST(req_id VARCHAR2(4), acct_no VARCHAR2(8), amount NUMBER(14,2))
RTGS_OUT(req_id VARCHAR2(4), acct_no VARCHAR2(8), amount NUMBER(14,2) CHECK (amount >= 200000))
RTGS_REJECT(req_id VARCHAR2(4), reason VARCHAR2(30))
-- a CHECK violation raises ORA-02290

questions.simple: Think of a ticket counter with a sign: 'Only tickets above 200 rupees here'. If someone asks for a cheaper ticket, the clerk writes their name in a 'sent away' notebook and serves the next person. EXCEPTION_INIT gives the database's rule-break error a friendly name, so our code can catch exactly that problem and keep going.

The inner BEGIN-EXCEPTION-END block handles the error per row, so only the failed INSERT is undone by statement-level rollback and the loop continues. Any other error is not caught and propagates, which is safer than WHEN OTHERS.

questions.title: New sanctions hits since yesterday
questions.scenario: AML officer Imran Qureshi gets a daily list of customers who hit the sanctions watchlist. He wants alerts only for customers who are new today, not repeats from yesterday.
questions.schema:
CREATE TYPE t_ids AS TABLE OF VARCHAR2(6);  -- schema-level nested table type

MULTISET operators work on nested tables only, not associative arrays, and the result is densely filled, so FORALL 1 .. COUNT is safe. FORALL then sends all inserts to the SQL engine in one context switch.
questions.tip: For set logic on PL/SQL collections, I use MULTISET UNION, INTERSECT or EXCEPT on nested tables instead of nested loops.

questions.scenario: Card product head Neha Kapoor compares how strongly each new credit card variant started. Issuance is reported per region, so a launch month can have several rows.
questions.schema:
CARD_ISSUE(card_variant VARCHAR2(15), region VARCHAR2(10), issue_month DATE, cards_issued NUMBER(8))
-- issue_month is the 1st of the month; one row per variant, region and month
questions.output_note: RUPAY_PLAT launched in August across two regions: 700 + 500 = 1200. Its big September month is ignored.

questions.hint: First SUM per variant and month, then ROW_NUMBER by issue_month and keep row 1.

  SELECT card_variant, issue_month, SUM(cards_issued) AS issued
  FROM card_issue
  GROUP BY card_variant, issue_month
), r AS (
  SELECT m.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY card_variant
                                 ORDER BY issue_month) AS rn
  FROM m
)

FROM r
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY issued DESC;
questions.simple: Think of a new shop that opens branches in two towns in the same month. To know how good the opening month was, you add both towns' sales for that first month only. The query first adds up regions for each month, then picks each card's very first month, then sorts the best start on top.
questions.remember: Aggregate first, then pick the first month.
questions.why: Picking the first row before aggregating would return only one region (700 or 500) for RUPAY_PLAT, so the CTE m sums across regions per variant and month first. ROW_NUMBER over issue_month ascending marks the launch month per variant, and rn = 1 keeps it. MIN(issue_month) with a join back is an alternative, but the window approach scans once.
questions.tip: In "first period" questions, I aggregate to the right grain before ranking, otherwise I rank partial rows.

questions.title: Net settlement between bank pairs
questions.scenario: Treasury analyst Vikram Shetty settles interbank payments once a day. Instead of paying both ways, each pair of banks should settle one net amount, and pairs that cancel out need no payment.
questions.schema:
INTERBANK_PAY(pay_id VARCHAR2(4), from_bank VARCHAR2(4), to_bank VARCHAR2(4), amount NUMBER(15,2))
-- from_bank owes to_bank the amount (INR); bank codes like SBIN, HDFC, ICIC
questions.output_note: SBIN owes HDFC 5000000 + 700000 and is owed 3200000, so it pays 2500000 net. ICIC and SBIN cancel to 0 and are dropped.
questions.task: For each pair of banks, compute the net amount owed. Show payer, payee and net_amount for pairs with a non-zero net, largest first.
questions.hint: Use LEAST and GREATEST to make one key per pair, sign the amount by direction, then SUM.
questions.solution:
WITH p AS (
  SELECT LEAST(from_bank, to_bank)    AS bank_a,
         GREATEST(from_bank, to_bank) AS bank_b,
         CASE WHEN from_bank < to_bank
              THEN amount ELSE -amount END AS signed_amt
  FROM interbank_pay
), n AS (
  SELECT bank_a, bank_b, SUM(signed_amt) AS net
  FROM p
  GROUP BY bank_a, bank_b
)
SELECT CASE WHEN net > 0 THEN bank_a ELSE bank_b END AS payer,
       CASE WHEN net > 0 THEN bank_b ELSE bank_a END AS payee,
       ABS(net) AS net_amount
FROM n
WHERE net <> 0
ORDER BY net_amount DESC;
questions.simple: Imagine you owe your friend 50 rupees and your friend owes you 32. Instead of swapping money twice, you just give 18. The query puts each pair of banks in alphabetical order so 'A to B' and 'B to A' land in the same box. Money one way is plus, the other way is minus, and the total tells who pays whom.
questions.remember: LEAST and GREATEST = one key for both directions.
questions.why: LEAST and GREATEST normalise (SBIN, HDFC) and (HDFC, SBIN) into the same ordered key, so both directions group together. The CASE gives a positive sign when bank_a pays bank_b and negative otherwise, so SUM is the net exposure of bank_a to bank_b. The final CASE uses the sign to choose payer and payee, ABS makes the amount positive, and net <> 0 removes pairs that fully offset.
questions.tip: For A-to-B versus B-to-A problems, I build an unordered pair key with LEAST/GREATEST and a signed amount.

Step two. Money from the first bank to the second is plus. The other way is minus.

steps.say: Step three. Add up the signed amounts for each pair to get the net.

steps.say: Finally, the sign decides who pays. Pairs that cancel to zero are dropped.

questions.title: When did Ramayana cross 500 crore?
questions.scenario: Neha works in analytics at a bank that processes a cinema chain's ticket payments. Her manager wants the day the film's India collection crossed 500 crore rupees, to plan a 500 crore club cashback offer. The numbers below are sample data.
questions.schema:
BOX_OFFICE(show_date DATE, collection_cr NUMBER(8,2))
-- one row per day, India collection in crore rupees (sample data)
questions.output_note: On 10 Nov the total went from 465 to 525, so only that day is marked. 11 Nov is above 500 too, but the day before was already above 500.
questions.task: Show each day's collection with a running total, and mark the first day the running total reached 500 crore as 'CROSSED 500'.
questions.hint: SUM() OVER (ORDER BY show_date) keeps adding day by day; running total minus today's value is yesterday's total.
questions.solution:
SELECT show_date, collection_cr,
       SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) AS running_total_cr,
       CASE WHEN SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) >= 500
             AND SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) - collection_cr < 500
            THEN 'CROSSED 500' END AS milestone
FROM   box_office
ORDER  BY show_date;
questions.simple: It is like filling a piggy bank every day. Each day you add that day's money and check the total. On 10 November the total jumped from 465 to 525, so that is the day it crossed 500. The CASE checks two things: today's total is 500 or more, and yesterday's total was below 500.
questions.remember: Running total = SUM with OVER ORDER BY.
questions.why: SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) uses the default frame RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, giving a cumulative sum. Subtracting the current row's value gives the previous running total, so the crossing day is where the previous total is below 500 and the current one is at least 500. No self-join or subquery is needed.
questions.tip: Running total minus today's value gives yesterday's total, so I can find the exact crossing day without a self-join.

trend.hook: Ramayana is ruling the box office, so let's find the day it crossed 500 crore!

steps.say: Step one. SUM with OVER, ORDER BY show date, adds each day's collection to the total so far.
steps.find: SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) AS running_total_cr

steps.say: Step two. CASE checks that today's running total is five hundred or more.
And that yesterday's total, which is the running total minus today, was still below five hundred.
Only that one day gets the label CROSSED 500.
Finally, ORDER BY show date lists the days in order.

questions.title: GTA 6 pre-orders: which cities make 80%?
questions.scenario: Arjun runs card-offers at a bank whose cards were used for GTA 6 pre-orders. He wants the smallest set of cities that together bring 80 percent of pre-order revenue, to target a cashback campaign there. The numbers are sample data.
questions.schema:
GTA6_PREORDERS(order_id VARCHAR2(5), city VARCHAR2(30), platform VARCHAR2(10), amount_inr NUMBER(8))
-- one row per pre-order paid with the bank's cards (sample data)
questions.output_note: Delhi is included because the total was still below 80 percent before it (63.3). Bengaluru and Delhi tie on revenue, so city name breaks the tie.
questions.task: Show the cities, biggest revenue first, that together make up 80 percent of pre-order revenue, including the city that crosses 80 percent, with the cumulative percentage.
questions.hint: Group by city first, then a running SUM over revenue descending; keep cities whose running total before them was below 80 percent.
questions.solution:
SELECT city, revenue,
       ROUND(100 * running / total, 1) AS cum_pct
FROM (
  SELECT city, SUM(amount_inr) AS revenue,
         SUM(SUM(amount_inr)) OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount_inr) DESC, city
                                    ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running,
         SUM(SUM(amount_inr)) OVER () AS total
  FROM gta6_preorders
  GROUP BY city
)
WHERE running - revenue < 0.8 * total
ORDER BY revenue DESC, city;
questions.simple: Line up the cities from richest to poorest, like children lining up by height. Walk down the line adding up their money. Keep going until you have 80 percent of all the money, and include the city that takes you past 80. Everyone after that is left out.
questions.remember: Pareto = running SUM sorted big to small.
questions.why: The inner query groups to city revenue, and SUM(SUM(amount_inr)) OVER (...) runs a window over the grouped rows. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING plus city in ORDER BY makes tied cities add one at a time; the default RANGE frame would add tied rows together. running - revenue is the total before the current city, so the filter keeps the crossing city too.
questions.tip: I always add ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to running totals, because the default RANGE frame lumps tied values together.

trend.hook: GTA 6 is finally out, so let's see which cities spent the most on pre-orders!

steps.say: Step one. Inside, GROUP BY city adds up each city's pre-order revenue.
A window SUM over revenue, biggest first, gives the running total. ROWS makes tied cities count one at a time.
An empty OVER gives the grand total of all cities.
Step two. Keep a city if the total before it was still below eighty percent.
Finally, running divided by total gives the cumulative percentage.

questions.concept: Peak hour per group with RANK
questions.title: Avengers: Doomsday peak booking hour per city
questions.scenario: Priya in the bank's payments team watches card traffic when Avengers: Doomsday advance booking opened. She needs the busiest hour in each city, to plan server capacity for the next big release. The numbers are sample data.
questions.schema:
AD_BOOKINGS(booking_id VARCHAR2(5), city VARCHAR2(30), booked_at DATE, seats NUMBER(3))
-- one row per advance booking paid by card (sample data)
questions.output_note: Chennai has a tie (5 seats at 10 and at 11), so RANK keeps both hours.
questions.task: For each city, show the hour (HH24) with the most seats booked and the seats in that hour. If two hours tie, show both.
questions.hint: Group by city and hour, then RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) and keep rank 1.
questions.solution:
SELECT city, booking_hour, seats
FROM (
  SELECT city,
         TO_CHAR(booked_at, 'HH24') AS booking_hour,
         SUM(seats) AS seats,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city
                      ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM ad_bookings
  GROUP BY city, TO_CHAR(booked_at, 'HH24')
)
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY city, booking_hour;
questions.simple: Think of a sports day where each school gets its own race. We count the seats booked in every hour, then hold a separate race inside each city. The hour with the most seats wins in that city. If two hours finish together, both get the gold medal, which is what RANK does.
questions.remember: Best per group = RANK OVER PARTITION BY, keep 1.
questions.why: GROUP BY city and TO_CHAR(booked_at, 'HH24') gives seats per city-hour. RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) restarts numbering in each city and gives tied hours the same rank, so rnk = 1 returns all top hours. ROW_NUMBER would silently drop one of the tied hours.
questions.tip: I pick RANK over ROW_NUMBER when ties must all be shown, and say so in the interview.

trend.hook: Avengers: Doomsday bookings are open, so let's find the busiest booking hour!

steps.say: Step one. Inside, group by city and booking hour, and add up the seats.
RANK with PARTITION BY city starts a new race in every city, most seats first.
steps.to: ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) AS rnk

steps.say: The GROUP BY must use the same hour expression.
Step two. Keep only rank one. Tied hours both have rank one, so both stay.
Finally, sort by city and hour.

lessons.why: LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value unless you widen the window, a common bug in month-end and closing-rate reports.
lessons.explain: When an analytic function has ORDER BY but no frame, Oracle uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. For SUM that gives a running total, but for LAST_VALUE it means the last row seen so far is the current row, so you get the row's own value back. To get the true last value of the partition, state ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY ... DESC. Adding IGNORE NULLS turns it into a carry-forward tool.
lessons.example:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-02' d, 83.10 rate FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-03', 83.25 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-04', 83.18 FROM dual
)
SELECT d, rate,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS default_frame,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS closing_rate
FROM r;
-- default_frame: 83.10, 83.25, 83.18   closing_rate: 83.18, 83.18, 83.18
lessons.gotcha: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) looks right in a quick test but just echoes x on every row.
lessons.line: For a closing value per period I use LAST_VALUE with an explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame, or FIRST_VALUE ordered descending, because the default frame stops at the current row.
lessons.simple: LAST_VALUE sounds like 'give me the last one', but by default it only looks from the top down to the current row, so the last one it sees is itself. To see the real last row, tell it to look all the way to the end.
lessons.remember: Tell LAST_VALUE to look to the end: UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

lessons.why: Top-N queries written with ROWNUM in the same SELECT as ORDER BY return the wrong rows, a classic interview trap and a real reporting bug.
lessons.simple: Imagine a teacher who hands out medals to the first 2 children who walk in, and only after that lines them up by height. The medal winners were never the tallest, just the first through the door. ROWNUM is that door number: Oracle gives it out before ORDER BY sorts. So sort first in an inner query, then hand out the numbers.
lessons.remember: ROWNUM is given before sorting; sort inside, filter outside.
lessons.explain: ROWNUM is assigned to each row as it passes the WHERE clause, before ORDER BY runs, so WHERE ROWNUM <= 2 ... ORDER BY bal DESC picks any two rows and then sorts just those. The fix is to sort in an inline view and apply ROWNUM outside it, or in 12c and later use ORDER BY ... FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY (or ROW_NUMBER() OVER for top-N per group). WHERE ROWNUM > 1 never returns anything, because the first row fails, so the next row becomes ROWNUM 1 again. FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES also keeps rows tied with the last one.
lessons.gotcha: SELECT ... WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY amount DESC returns five random rows sorted, not the top five.
lessons.line: Because ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY, I either sort in an inline view and filter ROWNUM outside, or simply use FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY.

lessons.why: Picking the wrong ranking function on tied values is one of the most common interview traps in top-N and Nth-highest questions.
lessons.simple: Think of a race where two runners cross the line together. ROW_NUMBER is the strict referee who still gives them 1 and 2. RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 3, skipping 2. DENSE_RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 2, without skipping. All three just put numbers on rows in the order you ask for.
lessons.remember: ROW_NUMBER unique, RANK skips, DENSE_RANK never skips.
lessons.explain: All three are analytic functions that need OVER (ORDER BY ...) and can restart per group with PARTITION BY. ROW_NUMBER always gives 1, 2, 3 even on ties, so which tied row gets the lower number is not deterministic unless you add a tie-breaker column. RANK gives tied rows the same number and then jumps (1, 1, 3), while DENSE_RANK gives the same number and continues (1, 1, 2). Use ROW_NUMBER for de-duplication or exactly-N rows, RANK for 'positions' like a competition, and DENSE_RANK for 'Nth highest distinct value'.
lessons.example:
WITH b AS (
  SELECT 'Arun' cust, 90000 bal FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Bina', 90000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Chetan', 70000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Divya', 50000 FROM dual
)
SELECT cust, bal,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC, cust) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS drnk
FROM   b;
-- Arun 90000 1 1 1 | Bina 90000 2 1 1 | Chetan 70000 3 3 2 | Divya 50000 4 4 3
lessons.gotcha: Using ROW_NUMBER = 1 to find 'the top customer' silently drops a customer who is tied for first place.
lessons.line: I pick ROW_NUMBER when I need exactly one row per group, RANK when ties should share a position with gaps, and DENSE_RANK for Nth-highest distinct values.

lessons.why: Interviewers often ask for a total next to each detail row, and choosing GROUP BY instead of an analytic function loses the detail rows.
lessons.simple: Think of a class photo and a class report card. GROUP BY is the report card: one line per class with the total, and the children's names disappear. OVER (PARTITION BY) is the class photo with a sticker on each child showing the class total: every child is still there. Use GROUP BY for summaries and OVER when you need the details plus the total.
lessons.remember: GROUP BY squashes rows; OVER keeps every row.
lessons.explain: GROUP BY collapses all rows with the same key into one result row, so only grouped columns and aggregates can be selected. An analytic function such as SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY branch) computes the same aggregate but returns it on every input row, without reducing the row count. Analytic functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING but before the final ORDER BY, so they cannot be used in WHERE; wrap them in an inline view to filter. You can even combine both, for example SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () to get a grand total next to grouped rows.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT 'Pune' branch, 'A1' acct, 5000 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Pune', 'A2', 3000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Nagpur', 'A3', 7000 FROM dual
)
SELECT branch, acct, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY branch) AS branch_total,
       ROUND(100 * amt / SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY branch), 1) AS pct
FROM   t
ORDER  BY branch, acct;
-- Nagpur A3 7000 7000 100 | Pune A1 5000 8000 62.5 | Pune A2 3000 8000 37.5
lessons.gotcha: Putting an analytic function in the WHERE clause raises ORA-30483; filter on it in an outer query instead.
lessons.line: I use GROUP BY when I want one row per group, and SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) when I need the group total alongside every detail row.

lessons.why: Interviewers often ask when to use EXISTS or IN, and the NOT IN version silently returns nothing when the list has a NULL.
lessons.simple: Think of a teacher asking 'is there at least one homework copy from Ravi in the pile?'. EXISTS stops looking as soon as it finds one copy, it just answers yes or no. IN first makes a list of names from the pile and checks if Ravi is on it. For finding matches both give the same answer. For 'not in the pile', a blank name on the list confuses NOT IN, but NOT EXISTS still works.
lessons.remember: EXISTS asks 'any match?'; NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe.
lessons.explain: EXISTS (correlated subquery) returns TRUE as soon as one matching row is found, and the select list inside it is ignored, so SELECT 1 is common. IN compares a value with the set returned by the subquery; for positive checks Oracle usually rewrites both into the same semi-join, so performance is often identical. The difference shows with negation: if the subquery returns any NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never TRUE and the query returns no rows, whereas NOT EXISTS is evaluated row by row and is unaffected. Oracle turns NOT EXISTS (and NOT IN on NOT NULL columns) into an anti-join.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2' FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3' FROM dual
), upi_txn AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 500 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL, 900 FROM dual
)
SELECT a.acct_no,
       CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM upi_txn u WHERE u.acct_no = a.acct_no)
            THEN 'Uses UPI' ELSE 'No UPI' END AS upi_status
FROM   acct a
ORDER  BY a.acct_no;
-- A1 Uses UPI | A2 No UPI | A3 No UPI
-- But WHERE acct_no NOT IN (SELECT acct_no FROM upi_txn) returns no rows because of the NULL.
lessons.gotcha: NOT IN against a subquery that can return NULL gives an empty result, so use NOT EXISTS or add WHERE col IS NOT NULL inside.
lessons.line: For positive checks IN and EXISTS usually get the same semi-join plan, but for exclusions I write NOT EXISTS because NOT IN breaks when the subquery returns a NULL.

lessons.why: Interviewers like asking the difference between NVL and COALESCE, and getting it right shows you understand NULL handling and performance.
lessons.simple: Think of a shopping bill where some prices are blank. NVL says 'if the box is empty, write this instead'. NVL2 asks 'is the box filled?' and writes one word for yes and another for no. COALESCE looks along a row of boxes and takes the first one that is filled. All three help you put something sensible where a blank would be.
lessons.remember: NVL = one backup, COALESCE = first filled box.
lessons.explain: NVL(a, b) returns b when a is NULL and always evaluates both arguments, converting b to the data type of a. NVL2(a, b, c) returns b when a is NOT NULL and c when it is NULL, which is handy for flags. COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) is ANSI standard, accepts any number of arguments, returns the first non-NULL one and stops evaluating as soon as it finds it (short-circuit). COALESCE requires all arguments to be of the same data type family, so COALESCE(number_col, 'NA') raises ORA-00932 where NVL would try an implicit conversion.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 5000 od_limit, CAST(NULL AS NUMBER) temp_limit FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2', NULL, 20000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3', NULL, NULL FROM dual
)
SELECT acct_no,
       NVL(od_limit, 0)                   AS od_or_zero,
       NVL2(od_limit, 'Has OD', 'No OD')  AS od_flag,
       COALESCE(temp_limit, od_limit, 0)  AS effective_limit
FROM   acct
ORDER  BY acct_no;
-- A1 5000 Has OD 5000 | A2 0 No OD 20000 | A3 0 No OD 0
lessons.gotcha: NVL always evaluates its second argument, so NVL(col, slow_function()) calls the function for every row, while COALESCE calls it only when col is NULL.
lessons.line: I prefer COALESCE because it is ANSI, takes many arguments and short-circuits, and I use NVL2 when I need a different value for filled and empty cases.

lessons.why: Banks run the same query millions of times, and interviewers ask about bind variables to see if you can avoid a common cause of slow, CPU-hungry databases.
lessons.simple: Think of a shopping bill printed from a template where only the name and amount change. If the shop designed a brand-new bill layout for every customer, it would be very slow. A literal like acct_no = 'A1' makes Oracle plan a new query each time. A bind variable like acct_no = :acct lets Oracle reuse the same plan and just fill in the blank.
lessons.remember: Same query, new value? Use a :bind, reuse the plan.
lessons.explain: Before running a SQL statement Oracle parses it and builds an execution plan, and a hard parse (syntax check, optimisation, plan creation) is expensive and takes shared pool latches. If the SQL text differs only by a literal value, each version is a new statement and needs its own hard parse, filling the shared pool with near-duplicates. With a bind variable the text stays the same, so later executions are soft parses that reuse the cached cursor; static SQL in PL/SQL binds variables automatically, and dynamic SQL should use EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ... USING. Bind variables also prevent SQL injection, because the value is never part of the SQL text.
lessons.example:
VARIABLE acct VARCHAR2(10)
EXEC :acct := 'A2'

WITH account AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 52000 balance FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2', 18500 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3', 730000 FROM dual
)
SELECT acct_no, balance
FROM   account
WHERE  acct_no = :acct;
-- A2 18500 ; change :acct and rerun, the same cursor is reused
lessons.gotcha: Concatenating values into dynamic SQL ('... WHERE acct_no = ''' || p_acct || '''') gives a new hard parse per value and opens a SQL injection hole, so use USING binds instead.
lessons.line: I use bind variables so repeated statements are soft-parsed and share one cursor, which saves CPU and protects against SQL injection.

lessons.concept: When Oracle can use a B-tree index
lessons.why: Bank tables hold crores of rows, and interviewers check whether you know why a query on an indexed column can still scan the whole table.
lessons.simple: Think of the index at the back of a textbook: words are listed A to Z with page numbers, so you jump straight to the page. If you ask 'find words that end in -tion', the A-to-Z list cannot help and you must read every page. An Oracle index works the same way on the column's real stored values. If you change the column first (wrap it in a function, or compare text to a number), Oracle cannot use the list and reads the whole table.
lessons.remember: Leave the indexed column bare; change the value instead.
lessons.explain: A B-tree index stores column values in sorted order with ROWIDs, so Oracle can do an index range scan when the predicate compares the bare column with =, <, >, BETWEEN or a LIKE with a fixed prefix. Wrapping the column in a function such as TRUNC(txn_date) or UPPER(name), a leading wildcard LIKE '%1001', or an implicit conversion (acct_no VARCHAR2 compared with the number 1001 becomes TO_NUMBER(acct_no) = 1001) hides the stored values, so the optimizer cannot use a normal index. The fix is to rewrite the predicate on the value side (txn_date >= :d AND txn_date < :d + 1, acct_no = '1001') or create a function-based index on the exact expression. Even a usable index may be skipped if the query returns a large share of rows, because a full scan with multiblock reads is then cheaper.
lessons.example:
WITH txn AS (
  SELECT '1001' acct_no, TO_DATE('31-03-2026 10:15','DD-MM-YYYY HH24:MI') txn_date, 5000 amount FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT '1001', TO_DATE('31-03-2026 18:40','DD-MM-YYYY HH24:MI'), 1200 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT '1002', TO_DATE('01-04-2026 09:05','DD-MM-YYYY HH24:MI'), 800 FROM dual
)
SELECT acct_no, txn_date, amount
FROM   txn
WHERE  acct_no  = '1001'                  -- not acct_no = 1001
AND    txn_date >= DATE '2026-03-31'       -- not TRUNC(txn_date) = ...
AND    txn_date <  DATE '2026-04-01';
-- returns the two rows of 31-03-2026 for account 1001
lessons.gotcha: Comparing a VARCHAR2 column to a number makes Oracle apply TO_NUMBER to every row's column, which silently disables the index and can even raise ORA-01722 on non-numeric values.
lessons.line: I keep indexed columns bare in WHERE clauses, match data types to avoid implicit conversion, and use function-based indexes only when the expression cannot be moved to the value side.

lessons.why: Interviewers ask which column goes first in a multi-column index, and the answer decides whether your query uses it.
lessons.simple: Think of a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. Finding all 'Sharma' is fast, and 'Sharma, Ritu' is even faster. But finding every 'Ritu' means reading the whole book. A composite index is the same: it helps when you search by its first column.
lessons.remember: Leading column first: the index is sorted by it.
lessons.explain: A composite B-tree index on (acct_no, txn_date) is sorted by acct_no, then txn_date inside each acct_no. Queries filtering on acct_no, or acct_no plus a txn_date range, can do a fast range scan. A filter on txn_date alone cannot seek directly; Oracle may use an index skip scan only if acct_no has few distinct values, otherwise a full scan. Put equality-filtered columns first and range-filtered columns after them.
lessons.example:
WITH txn AS (
  SELECT 'SB1' acct_no, DATE '2026-11-03' txn_date, 5000 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'SB1', DATE '2026-11-18', 1200 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'SB2', DATE '2026-11-05', 800 FROM dual
)
-- on a real table, an index on (acct_no, txn_date) serves this filter well
SELECT * FROM txn
WHERE acct_no = 'SB1'
  AND txn_date >= DATE '2026-11-01' AND txn_date < DATE '2026-12-01';
lessons.gotcha: An index on (acct_no, txn_date) does not help much a query that filters only on txn_date.
lessons.line: I put equality columns first and the range column last, so one index range scan answers the query.

lessons.why: A number compared with a text column can silently stop Oracle from using an index, a classic interview trap.
lessons.simple: Imagine a library where books are sorted by their written titles. If you ask for a book by a number, the librarian has to read every title and turn it into a number before comparing. That is slow. When a text column is compared with a number, Oracle does the same thing to every row.
lessons.remember: Compare text with text, numbers with numbers.
lessons.explain: When types differ, Oracle converts one side; between VARCHAR2 and NUMBER it converts the character side to NUMBER. So WHERE acct_no = 1001 on a VARCHAR2 column becomes TO_NUMBER(acct_no) = 1001, which is applied to every row and blocks a normal index on acct_no. It can also raise ORA-01722 if any row holds a non-numeric value like 'SB1001'. Writing acct_no = '1001' keeps the index usable, and dates should be compared with DATE or TO_DATE values, not strings.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT '1001' acct_no, 25000 bal FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT '1002', 8000 FROM dual
)
-- good: text compared with text, an index on acct_no can be used
SELECT * FROM acct
WHERE acct_no = '1001';
lessons.gotcha: WHERE acct_no = 1001 on a VARCHAR2 column can fail with ORA-01722 once a row like 'SB1001' arrives.
lessons.line: I match literal and bind types to the column type, because implicit TO_NUMBER on the column disables its index.
